AN 'ADDRESS-TAKEN SUB-STRUCTURE' MAY JUST BE AN ARRAY BASE. Guard 8 correctly found +0x90 and +0x94 but iteration 78 read them as pointers to sub-objects. Reading six instructions further showed three post-indexed walks over 2-element int16 arrays. Address-taken tells you the offset, not the shape -- read the loop before naming it.

RULE OUT A COINCIDENTAL OFFSET BY CODE VOLUME, NOT BY INTUITION. The two BattleCol.cpp +0x90 sites span 1320 bytes and touch ZERO of the record's twelve signature offsets. That quantity is the argument; 'it is probably a different struct' is not.

WRONG IS WORSE THAN BLIND. Iteration 79 called post-indexed addressing a blind spot in every scanner. struct_fields.py was not blind -- it decoded those instructions and got them wrong, emitting a confident phantom field (+0x9A) into a published map. A gap announces itself as a gap; a wrong decode looks like a finding. When auditing a tool, check what it does with an input class, not just whether it sees it.

AN ADDRESSING MODE IS PART OF THE OFFSET'S MEANING. `[r6],#2` is not offset 2. P, U and W change what the immediate means -- stride vs offset, add vs subtract -- and ignoring them yields plausible-looking numbers rather than errors. Decode the mode bits before trusting any offset.

A TRANSFER CAN WRITE ITS OWN BASE, INCLUDING A STORE. Guard 2 checked only the destination register of loads, so `str r0,[r4],#4` slipped through and the walk continued with a base that had already moved. Any writeback form must count as a write to the base.

AN IMPLAUSIBLE PROPORTION IS A FREE CORRECTNESS CHECK. The measurement script first said 97.5% of transfers were post-indexed -- impossible, so the byte-order bug got caught. A plausible wrong number would have gone straight into the doc. Sanity-check every proportion against what the answer ought to look like before reporting it.

A REGEX OVER ARM MNEMONICS SILENTLY DROPS EVERY PREDICATED INSTRUCTION. `strne` does not match an alternation containing `str`, and nothing warns. On one sweep that hid 19 of 47 stores -- 40%. ARM is dense with conditional execution by design. Decode the word; the condition is bits 31-28 and the transfer encoding underneath is identical.

THE BUG YOU SET OUT TO FIX MAY NOT BE THE BUG THAT MATTERS. This wake was queued to port three addressing-mode fixes. Those contributed ZERO new sites; condition codes contributed 19. Porting the fix was still right, but the audit that came with it is what paid.

WHEN REPLACING A SCANNER, MEASURE GAINED AND LOST SEPARATELY. 'Gained 19, lost 0' is what makes the new decoder trustworthy -- a strict superset means no earlier reasoning silently evaporated. A single 'now finds 47' would not have shown that.

RE-RUN THE LOAD-BEARING RESULT AFTER FIXING THE TOOL THAT PRODUCED IT. B11's vestigial-field conclusion came from the old scanner. Re-running it on the corrected one -- same 2 sites, same refutations -- is what lets the conclusion stand rather than needing an asterisk.

A PREDICTED BUG THAT DOES NOT FIRE IS STILL WORTH THE WAKE. alloc_census.py really did have the condition-suffix flaw, and fixing it changed nothing -- 494/431/469/63 all identical. That negative CONFIRMS the tagged-allocation naming from iterations 73 and 77 instead of leaving it under suspicion. Verifying a load-bearing number is not wasted effort just because it holds.

WORD MASKS THAT EXCLUDE THE CONDITION NIBBLE ARE IMMUNE BY CONSTRUCTION. find_jump_tables.py uses 0x0FFFFFF0, so bits 31-28 never enter the comparison and every predicated form matches for free. Prefer a mask that deliberately ignores the condition over a regex that must enumerate 15 suffixes.

A TIGHT MASK IS A FEATURE WHEN THE INPUT INCLUDES DATA. Ten `pc`-writing 'dispatches' visible to a loose text scan were pointer-table words misdecoded as instructions. Requiring `lsl #2` exactly rejected all ten. Loosening a pattern to raise recall raises the false-positive rate against data regions first.

NEVER DROP A RESULT BECAUSE A SECONDARY ATTRIBUTE IS MISSING. find_jump_tables.py discarded any dispatch whose case count it could not recover -- no filter requested, no mention in the output. Two real unconditional jump tables were absent from every run for that reason. Report the site and mark the attribute unknown.

SCOPE BY MODULE WHEN THE COMPANION LIST GOES SOFT. Searching +0x68 writers by companion offsets returned 55 sites and a dozen false MATCHes, because +0x50/+0x5c/+0x60/+0x6c are common. Restricting to the collision modules' address range gave exactly ONE store -- the right one. Address scope is a discriminator too, and sometimes the better one.

A LIST HEAD FOUND ONCE IS NOT THE ONLY LIST HEAD. Iteration 78 recorded record+0x08 as 'the' node list from a single allocator site. The detach routine walks three more at +0x10/+0x18/+0x20 in a strided loop. A struct with one observed list usually has more; look for a loop that strides over heads before declaring the count.

A STRIDED LOOP OVER STRUCT OFFSETS IS A FIELD-GROUP DECLARATION. `add r6,sl,#0x10` then `add r6,r6,#8` with `cmp r8,#3` says: three adjacent list heads, 8 bytes apart. That is more informative than three separate accesses would be, and no offset scan reports it -- it takes reading the loop.

TEARDOWN CODE IS THE BEST MAP OF OWNERSHIP. One detach routine gave three list heads, their node types, their free destinations, the bucket-array width, a flags bit, and the lifecycle hook -- because freeing an object requires touching everything it owns. Constructors scatter; destructors enumerate.

BOUND THE SEARCH BY WHAT CAN REACH THE STRUCT AT ALL. A ROM-wide sweep for +0x68 gave 55 stores and no answer. Noting that only 10240 words of code ever see the ColPrm global turned it into an exhaustive enumeration -- 9 write instructions of any form, each checkable by hand. Find the code that could possibly hold a pointer to the struct before searching for writes to it.

ENUMERATE WRITE FORMS, NOT JUST THE COMMON ONE. 'No direct store' is weak; 'one direct store, four register-offset, two stm, two post-indexed, all listed and none able to reach the offset' is a proof. The blind-spot classes catalogued at iterations 76 and 80 became the checklist that made this exhaustive.

A NULL GUARD IS EVIDENCE ABOUT THE FIELD. `cmp r2,#0; beq` around 26 instructions says the designers expected the field to be optional. Combined with no setter, it says the branch never runs. Read the guard as data, not boilerplate.

STATE WHICH NEIGHBOURING RESULTS A DEAD-CODE FINDING DOES NOT TOUCH. Declaring the partner walk dead could be misread as retracting iteration 83's four list heads. They sit on the fallthrough path. Saying so explicitly costs one line and prevents a later wake from re-deriving them.

A STRIDED POINTER WALK HIDES AN ENTIRE FIELD GROUP FROM AN ANCHOR-REGISTER SCAN. One pointer set to the first list head and advanced by 8 means only the first offset is ever expressed relative to the struct. Iteration 83 found +0x18/+0x20 by reading the loop; the tool needed a dedicated guard to see them. Whenever a scan reports exactly one list head, check for a stride.

A FORWARD BRANCH IS NOT A LOOP CLOSE, AND THE FIRST BACKWARD BRANCH MAY BE AN INNER LOOP. Both mistakes made the new guard return an empty list -- indistinguishable from 'nothing here'. Bottom-tested loops open with a forward jump to their condition, and a routine that drains a list per head closes the inner loop first.

ASSERT SPECIFIC VALUES IN A SELFTEST, NOT 'SOMETHING WAS FOUND'. Two consecutive bugs in guard 11 both yielded [], which a truthiness check would have passed as 'no strided group here'. Naming the three expected offsets is what caught them.

THE REAL TEST OF A TOOL IS REPRODUCING A HAND READING. Guard 11 is worth trusting because it independently derives the same +0x18/+0x20 that iteration 83 got by reading the disassembly. Build the hand result first, then make the tool match it.

A STORE'S BASE MAY BE UNIDENTIFIABLE WHILE A READER'S IS OBVIOUS. The prmData store writes [r6]+0x84 where r6 walks a descriptor array -- undecidable. A reader 0x02159AA0 loads +0x84 off a register that four instructions earlier loaded +0x1A0, a confirmed character field. When the writer's base is opaque, look for a reader whose base carries a known fingerprint.

RE-AUDITING A SUSPECT CLAIM CAN VINDICATE IT. Three offsets were flagged as ambiguous for thirteen wakes and all three resolved to the object the map originally named. The doubt was worth raising and worth closing; leaving it open was costing every downstream damage-pipeline claim an asterisk.

TWO OBJECTS IN ONE OVERLAY CAN SHARE A FIELD OFFSET. +0x84 is live on the battle character and the NoteTrack, both in ov6, both reachable from the same call graph. Seventh instance in this campaign. Offset reuse is not confined to different modules.

ANCHORING ON A CONSTRUCTOR'S ALLOCATION REGISTER IS THE STRONGEST STRUCT-IDENTITY EVIDENCE AVAILABLE. There is no ambiguity about what register holds the object right after the allocator returns. Sixteen character fields with no attribution risk came from two anchors chosen that way.

AN ADDRESS-TAKEN FIELD IS A VIEW, AN ARRAY, OR A SUB-REGION -- READ THE CALLEE TO TELL WHICH. Iteration 86 guessed 'array base'; the callees are three-instruction constructors that write back-pointers, making these embedded views. Two disassembly reads settled what a scan could only label.

COUNTING ADDRESS-TAKES RANKS A FIELD'S IMPORTANCE. char+0x130 is taken 29 times, char+0x120 four, char+0x7c five. That ratio pointed straight at the field worth following, and its consumers turned out to be the three biggest subsystems already on the map. Cheap to compute, strong as a prioritiser.

CONVERGENCE FROM SUBSYSTEMS MAPPED SEPARATELY IS REAL EVIDENCE. State dispatch, spawn dispatch and hit resolution were each mapped over different wakes with no knowledge of each other. Finding they all take the address of one embedded view is independent confirmation that the view matters -- and a hint that the three are more coupled than the map presents them.

`stm` USED AS A TWO-FIELD WRITE IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL. `stm r0,{r2,r3}` at 0x0215FB80 writes +0x0 and +0x4 of a real struct. The stm blind spot flagged at iterations 76 and 84 was justified: any offset scan would miss both fields here.

A STRING POOL IS A TABLE TERMINATOR. The handler table's extent was fixed by reading past it: index 16 decodes to 0x74746142 / 0x435F656C / 0x61726168 / 0x6F666E49 = "Battle_CharaInfo". Dumping a few words beyond a suspected table costs nothing and gives an exact length instead of a guess.

AN ADJACENT CONFIRMED FIELD BOUNDS AN EMBEDDED OBJECT'S SIZE. char+0x1A0 is a confirmed character field, so the view at char+0x130 cannot exceed 0x70 bytes. That upper bound refuted the appealing reading that the view IS Battle_CharaInfoCreate's 0xAC allocation -- same module, wrong instance. Embedded objects are sized by their neighbours, not by a constructor.

REPEATED `add rX, base, #OFF` FOLLOWED BY `mov r1, #N` IS A METHOD CALL WITH A SELECTOR. Ten sites that looked like ten separate uses were one idiom: pass the view, pass a small integer. Following the callee once explained all ten and produced the mask, the table and the array. Look for the shared shape before reading sites individually.

WATCH THE EDIT PASS FOR HEDGE REMOVAL ON UNVERIFIED READINGS. The opus-4-6 pass turned 'consistent with per-frame counters' into 'likely per-frame counters' -- a real strengthening of a claim with no evidence behind it. Concision editing is safe for prose but must not touch epistemic qualifiers; check them in the diff alongside the hex values.

THIRD MASK BUG WITH THE SAME SIGNATURE. `(y & 0x0FFF0000) == 0x03A01000` can never match: the mask zeroes bits 15-12 but the compare value sets them (Rd=1). Result: all 17 selectors reported COMPUTED -- clean, plausible, wrong. Same failure as iteration 46's BL mask and iteration 47's ldr mask. RULE: whenever a scan reports 100% of one category, verify the mask against one hand-decoded instruction before believing it.

TWO INDEPENDENT ROUTES TO THE SAME DEAD SET IS THE STRONGEST FORM OF THIS EVIDENCE. Table slots 0-3 share a no-op handler (iteration 88, from the table contents); selectors 0-3 are never issued (iteration 89, from the call sites). Neither observation depends on the other, and they coincide exactly -- which also refutes the reading that the shared handler is a live default.

'NO ISSUER' IS THE PRACTICAL DEFINITION OF A DEAD DISPATCH SLOT. Both ov6 dispatchers mapped so far (the 73-case one and this 16-entry one) were resolved by enumerating call sites and back-resolving the immediate, not by analysing the handlers. Cheaper and more decisive than reading the targets.

ONE ISSUER PER SELECTOR MEANS THESE ARE EVENTS, NOT AN API. Eleven of twelve live selectors are passed from exactly one function. A general-purpose interface would show reuse across callers; this shows each subsystem owning its own notification.

'FUNCTION IS DEAD' AND 'THIS ROUTE TO IT IS DEAD' ARE DIFFERENT CLAIMS. Iteration 46 correctly established dispatcher cases 23/24 as unreachable, and that quietly became 'SP-apply is dead code' in my working picture. It has four live callers through the view. When recording a dead path, name the path, not the destination.

A FIVE-INSTRUCTION HANDLER CAN CARRY THE WHOLE SEMANTICS. 0x0215FF4C is five instructions and it settles what the 16-slot table is for: index an int16 array by selector and apply it as SP to the character's data block. Reading the smallest handler first was worth more than reading the biggest.

SELECTOR RANGE FIXES ARRAY EXTENT. Selectors span 0-15, so an int16 array indexed by selector is exactly 0x20 bytes -- which places the array at +0x16 as ending at +0x35 and explains why the second one starts at +0x36. The dispatch range doubles as the array bound even though no bounds check exists in code.

A LITERAL-POOL SCAN CLASSIFIES HANDLERS CHEAPLY. Checking each of the 9 handlers for a nearby code-address literal split them instantly: 3 tail-call out of the module, 6 act on the view in place. That told me which to read for cross-subsystem effects and which for view semantics, before reading any of them.

A TWO-INSTRUCTION POINTER CHAIN CAN CLOSE A QUESTION THAT SURVIVED A DOZEN WAKES. The >=0x570 struct was hunted through allocation censuses and arm9 constructors for many iterations. Handler 0x0215FE14 reaches it with `ldr r0,[r5]; ldr r0,[r0,#0x56c]`. Reading small leaf functions in an unrelated subsystem found what targeted searches did not.

CROSS-CHECK A POINTER CHAIN AGAINST A KNOWN ANCHOR'S SHAPE, NOT JUST ITS ADDRESS. 0x0215FE14 and the GDB anchor 0x020784E4 both load +0x56c and then a signed halfword off the result. That shared shape -- not merely the shared offset -- is what makes the identification safe given how often offsets are reused here.

RECOUNT A TALLY BEFORE REPEATING IT. 'Nine unique handlers' was stated at iteration 88 and copied forward at 89 without recounting; the table has 11. The slot mapping was right both times, so the error was pure arithmetic -- exactly the kind that survives because it looks like a derived fact.

ADJACENT FIELDS WITH THE SAME SHAPE AND DIFFERENT CONSTANTS ARE ONE GROUP. +0x10, +0x12 and +0x14 are three halfword counters with caps 0x120, 0x1B0 and 0x2D0, each guarding a different handler. Found in three separate handlers across two wakes; only listing them together made the pattern visible.

TEST THE BIG CLAIM BEFORE WRITING IT, EVEN WHEN IT IS THE OBVIOUS READING. 'The arm function is unreachable, so the whole 16-slot table is dead' was the tidy conclusion. Checking it found 93 writers of +0xc in ov6 and showed the one strong candidate CLEARS the mask rather than setting it -- so the question is open, not closed. The doc says open.

A ZERO FROM xrefs-to IS NOT A ZERO. It reported no references at all for 0x0215FC20; a four-line raw word scan found the literal. Any conclusion resting on 'nothing references this' needs the raw scan, not the database.

AN IDEMPOTENT GUARD AT THE TOP OF A SETTER MARKS AN ARM/ONCE OPERATION. `tst mask, 1<<N; popne` says this function is designed to be called repeatedly and take effect once. That shape identified the function's role before any of its data flow was traced.

A FIELD INITIALISED TO ITS OWN COMPARISON CONSTANT IS A DISABLED-BY-DEFAULT SWITCH. The reset sets +0x12 = 0x1B0 and slot 15 compares +0x12 against 0x1B0 with bhs. Starting at the cap means the guarded path is skipped until something lowers it. Worth checking the other two counters' initial values for the same pattern.

AN `orr` SCAN DOES NOT COVER A WHOLE-WORD STORE. Eliminating the read-modify-write idiom felt like settling whether a mask is ever set -- but `mov rD,#0x1000; str rD,[base,#0xc]` sets bit 12 without any orr. Catching that gap before writing the conclusion is what kept the wake honest. Enumerate the ways a value can arrive, not just the idiomatic one.

RULE OUT CANDIDATES BY VALUE RANGE, NOT ONLY BY BASE. Two of five whole-word candidates died on arithmetic alone: 0x80000 is bit 19 and the selector space is 16 bits; 0x4B000 sets several bits at once. Checking the value against the field's known width is cheaper than tracing a base and just as decisive.

'NARROWED' IS A LEGITIMATE WAKE RESULT. Two wakes on the mask question have not closed it, but the candidate set went from 93 offset matches to two named sites plus two unresolvable write classes. Recording that precisely is more useful than either forcing a conclusion or reporting no progress.

A BIG NEGATIVE CLAIM NEEDS ITS RESIDUAL LISTED AS COUNTS, NOT ADJECTIVES. '1022 stm and 181 register-offset stores unresolved' tells the next wake exactly how much doubt remains and why scanning cannot remove it. 'Some routes remain unchecked' would not.

ENUMERATE WHERE THE POINTER CAN GO, NOT WHO WRITES THE OFFSET. Two wakes chasing writers of +0xc drowned in 93 offset matches, 1022 stm and 181 register-offset stores. Enumerating the view pointer's destinations instead gave a CLOSED set of 31 functions and settled the question in one pass. When an offset is common but the object is reached by few routes, invert the search.

A STORED POINTER COPY IS ONLY AN ESCAPE HATCH IF SOMETHING LOADS IT. char+0x120+0x0 holds the view pointer, which looked like it broke the enumeration -- until `ldr rD,[rB,#0x120]` returned ZERO sites in ov6. Check whether a stored copy is ever read before treating it as a leak.

AN 'UNRESOLVABLE' RESIDUAL CAN EVAPORATE UNDER A BETTER FRAME. Iteration 93 listed 1022 stm and 181 register-offset stores as permanently unscannable. They are irrelevant: any such write still needs a view pointer, and the pointers are enumerated. A residual is only as real as the question it attaches to.

FOUR VESTIGIAL SYSTEMS IS A PATTERN, NOT FOUR COINCIDENCES. ColPrm +0x68, +0xE8, +0x140 and now an entire 16-slot effect table with its data table and arm function. This build ships substantial machinery that is wired up and never switched on -- worth assuming as a live hypothesis when the next feature looks complete but unreachable.

EVERY CALLER ANALYSIS HERE HAS BEEN ARM-ONLY, AND AT LEAST ONE CONCLUSION DEPENDED ON IT. Battle_CharaCreate looked callerless because the scan could not see Thumb. The fix is a 20-line halfword scan for the Thumb BL/BLX pair. Any past finding of the form '0 callers, therefore a callback' or 'therefore unreachable' needs re-checking with it.

A CHECK THAT FINDS THE HIT YOU EXPECT *AND* THE ABSENCE YOU EXPECT IS WORTH MORE THAN EITHER. The Thumb scan found a caller for Battle_CharaCreate (where one must exist) and none for the arm function (where the ARM analysis said none). Both outcomes from one tool in one pass is what makes the second one credible.

VERIFY A DECODED HIT AGAINST THE ALTERNATIVE DECODING. A Thumb BL/BLX scan over ARM regions will manufacture calls from any matching halfword pair. What confirmed 0x0214D65E was the surrounding context -- `46c0` nop padding and a literal pool -- and that the ARM reading of the same bytes is incoherent.

CHECK A GLOBAL AGAINST ITS OVERLAY'S EXTENT BEFORE PLANNING TO READ IT. 0x02172984 sits 0x24 bytes past ov6's end, so it is BSS and the table behind it is runtime-only. One range comparison turned a queued task into a correctly-labelled blocked one.

AUDIT A NEWLY-FOUND BLIND SPOT ACROSS EVERY CLAIM THAT DEPENDED ON IT, IMMEDIATELY. One Thumb-only caller put nine conclusions in doubt. Checking all nine took one wake and found exactly one error -- which is worth far more than assuming either that they were all fine or that they all needed redoing.

A DECODER THAT CANNOT PRODUCE AN IMPOSSIBLE EDGE BEATS ONE THAT SCORES PLAUSIBILITY. The 'looks like Thumb nearby' heuristic passed hundreds of false edges. Two hard rules -- bl cannot switch state, and overlapping overlays are never co-resident -- rejected 499 of 686 with no judgement calls.

RANGE-BASED REGION RESOLUTION IS AMBIGUOUS IN THIS ROM, AND IT BROKE THE TOOL BUILT TO CATCH THAT. Ten overlays share 0x0214CD20, so resolving an address to a region returns whichever is checked first. The phantom filter therefore rejected its own hand-verified anchor as a phantom. Always use functions.json's declared provenance.

A SECOND INDEPENDENT CHECK ON A BIG NEGATIVE IS CHEAP ONCE THE TOOL EXISTS. The dead-handler-table result now rests on two separate arguments -- the enumerated pointer-holder set (iteration 94) and the absence of any Thumb caller for the arm function (iterations 95-96). Neither depends on the other.

BUILD THE MISSING DECODER RATHER THAN HAND-DECODING TWICE. Iteration 95 hand-decoded six Thumb instructions to verify one call; iteration 97 needed thirty more. A 170-line decoder with a selftest anchored on the already-verified six was cheaper than the second hand pass and makes every future Thumb question routine.

ANCHOR A NEW DECODER'S SELFTEST ON PREVIOUSLY HAND-VERIFIED OUTPUT. The six instructions read by hand at iteration 95 became the acceptance test. That is stronger than checking the decoder against itself, and it caught nothing this time only because the decoder was right -- which is exactly what the test is for.

A LOOP INDEX AS arg0 EXPLAINS A FIELD RECORDED THREE WAKES EARLIER. char+0x1E0 was logged at iteration 74 as `strb r6,[r4,#0x1e0]` from arg0, meaning nothing on its own. Seeing arg0 is a loop counter makes it the character's slot number. Argument provenance from the CALLER often names a field the callee cannot.

TWO LARGE WORD-INDEXED STRUCTS ARE NOT EVIDENCE OF BEING THE SAME STRUCT. r2 in the setup loop has fields at +0x104 and +0x158; the target struct is >=0x5F1. Tempting, and recorded as not claimed -- this campaign has produced eight coincidental offset collisions already.

ONE ARM-ONLY TOOL IMPLIES OTHERS -- CHECK THE WHOLE TOOLBOX. Iteration 95 found caller analysis was ARM-only; iteration 98 found the allocation census is too, missing 32% of allocations. After discovering an instruction-set assumption in one tool, audit every other tool built on the same assumption rather than waiting to trip over each one.

MEASURE A TOOLING GAP, THEN CHECK WHETHER IT ACTUALLY MOVED ANY CONCLUSION. 238 missed allocations sounds alarming; ov6 has three and none is large, so every battle finding that rested on the census survives. The gap and its consequences are separate questions and both deserve an answer.

AN OVERLAY'S ENTRY POINT IS ITS CONSTRUCTOR, AND ITS FIRST BSS WORD IS THE ROOT OBJECT. Battle_Add sits at ov6's first byte and stores its 0x170-byte allocation at 0x02172960, exactly where ov6's code ends. That pairing is worth checking first in any overlay rather than working inward from leaf functions.

REPORT A RESOLVER'S UNRELIABLE OUTPUT AS UNRELIABLE. My quick size back-resolver returned 0x214BE40 -- plainly a RAM address -- for several arm9 sites because it does not invalidate registers across calls. Flagging those as not-to-be-quoted costs a sentence; letting them into a table would put fake sizes into canon.

A BARE `except Exception` AROUND A LOADER TURNS A CODING ERROR INTO AN EMPTY RESULT. A missing import made the Thumb pass return zero sites for all 16 regions, reported as if the regions had no binaries. Same signature as this campaign's three mask bugs: clean, plausible, wrong. Catch only the errors that mean 'not present'.

A BACK-RESOLVER MUST TREAT MEMORY LOADS AS WRITES. `ldrh r0,[r4,#0x10]` does not look like it produces a value worth tracking, but it destroys one -- and a surviving stale `ldr r0,[pc,..]` became a reported allocation size of 0x214BE40, a RAM address. Enumerate every encoding that writes the register, not just the ones that set a value you can compute.

PUT A PLAUSIBILITY ASSERTION IN THE SELFTEST, NOT JUST AN ANCHOR. 'Battle_Add resolves to 0x170' would have passed with the stale-register bug intact. 'No Thumb size exceeds 0x100000' is what failed and forced the fix. Anchors catch regressions; range checks catch nonsense.

COMPLETING A TOOL'S COVERAGE IS ONLY HALF THE TASK -- RE-VERIFY WHAT DEPENDED ON IT. The census gained 238 sites; the useful output was confirming that none of the 12 allocations >= 0x570 is a battle object, so the finding that the [char+0x1b4] struct is not tagged-allocated now rests on complete data.

ONE CONSTRUCTOR CAN YIELD A WHOLE ARCHITECTURE. Battle_Add named 15 subsystems and placed 11 of them at fixed offsets in the module root -- more top-level structure than the previous twenty wakes of bottom-up field mapping produced. When a module has an entry point, read it before working inward from leaves.

A PARTIALLY-MATCHING IDIOM IS WORSE THAN NO MATCH. My extractor found `str r0,[r1,#0x0]` and reported eleven subsystems as living at offset +0x000 in their own globals. The real idiom has an `add r1,#OFF` in the middle. The output was uniform and plausible, which is exactly why it needed checking against the raw disassembly.

ABSENCE IN A CONSTRUCTOR IS STRUCTURAL INFORMATION. Battle_Add builds fifteen subsystems and none of the three collision managers. That says the collision layer has a separate initialisation path -- a concrete new question, obtained for free from a list of what was NOT called.

CROSS-REFERENCE CALLEES AGAINST THE SYMBOL TABLE BEFORE READING ANY OF THEM. 15 of 82 callees had assert-string names, and those 15 were the entire useful result. Filtering by 'has a name' turned 144 calls into a readable roster in one query.

WHEN A TOOL'S OUTPUT FEEDS A NEGATIVE CLAIM, THE TOOL'S COVERAGE *IS* THE CLAIM. 'No allocation >= 0x570 is a battle object' was really 'no allocation my resolver could size'. Three coverage bugs in this one tool in four wakes -- Thumb calls, stale registers, literal sizes -- and each time the headline number looked complete. Before resting a negative on a census, enumerate what the census cannot see.

LARGE CONSTANTS ARE LITERALS, SO A SIZE RESOLVER THAT ONLY READS IMMEDIATES IS BLIND TO EXACTLY THE BIGGEST OBJECTS. ARM's rotated immediate cannot express 0xFB54 or 0x42D8, so the compiler emits `ldr r0,[pc,..]`. The resolver's blind spot was perfectly correlated with what I was searching for.

READING ONE FUNCTION CAN FALSIFY A TOOL. Battle_ObjManCreate was queued as an engine question; its first six instructions exposed a census bug that overturned a conclusion from two wakes earlier. Reading real code remains the check on derived data.

SAY 'REOPENED' RATHER THAN QUIETLY DROPPING A REFUTED CLAIM. The >=0x5F1 struct being 'not tagged-allocated' was load-bearing for how I was searching for it. Marking it reopened -- with the seven new candidates listed -- is what keeps the next wake from re-deriving the wrong constraint.

AN EXACT ARITHMETIC FIT IS NOT EVIDENCE UNTIL THE CONSTANT APPEARS IN CODE. 0x1914 / 4 = 0x645 exactly, and 0x645 comfortably holds both known fields of the target struct. It took one query to find that 0x645 occurs nowhere in arm9 as an immediate or a literal. Divisibility is cheap; a stride the code actually uses is the claim.

READ HOW AN ARGUMENT IS BUILT INSTEAD OF TESTING CANDIDATES AGAINST IT. The plan was to check seven managers for two fields. Reading the eight instructions that construct the descriptor answered it outright -- [char+0x1b4] is an array element, so none of the seven could have been it. Provenance beats elimination.

ATTRIBUTE AN UNNAMED FUNCTION BY THE ALLOCATION TAGS THAT BRACKET IT. Neither +0x56c writer has an assert-string name, and the nearest named function was 0x1EB4 away and misleading. The tagged allocations at 0x02075FDC and 0x02078CFC bracket the module cleanly, and the GDB anchor falls inside the same range -- three independent addresses agreeing on ComicDeck.cpp.

A LONG-STANDING TENSION RESOLVING IS CORROBORATION, NOT PROOF. Per-player deck objects owning the SP gauge would explain the map's +0x558/+0x56c deck-wide-SP puzzle perfectly. Recorded as PLAUSIBLE -- the allocator of those objects is still unfound, and a satisfying story is exactly when to hold the line.

REFUTING A SPECIFIC FIT DOES NOT REFUTE THE GENERAL SHAPE. Iteration 102 correctly killed `0x1914 = 4 x 0x645` and then concluded the block is not four per-player decks. It IS four per-player slots -- with a 0x64 header and stride 0x61C. Kill the arithmetic, keep the hypothesis open.

A CONSTANT-SEARCH TEST CAN REJECT THE TRUTH. 0x61C is the real stride and appears nowhere in arm9 as an immediate or a literal, because it is built as #0x21C + #0x400. The same test that correctly rejected 0x645 would have rejected the right answer. Constant searches refute guesses; only reading the loop establishes a stride.

AN INITIALISER LOOP GIVES BASE, STRIDE AND COUNT IN ONE READ. Six instructions gave the header size, element size, element count and the list heads that follow -- everything a dozen wakes of field-by-field work could not. Find the constructor's clearing loop before mapping any array.

A FIELD FAR ABOVE A STRUCT'S SIZE IS A POINTER-HOP AWAY. char+0x558 sat in the map for a long time as an oddity on a 0x1F0 character. It belongs to the player slot at char+0x1b4. Any offset that exceeds a known struct size is a signal that the base was misattributed, not that the struct is bigger.

AN ADDRESS-TAKEN HIT INSIDE A CLEARING LOOP MAY BE LOOP ARITHMETIC. Guard 8 reported +0x21C as a field; it is half of the 0x61C stride. The guard cannot distinguish a field address from an induction variable, so any addr hit whose value equals part of a known stride deserves a second look.

WHERE THE FIELDS ARE *NOT* IS ALSO A RESULT. All 12 mapped offsets sit in the last 0xC4 bytes plus one at +0x058; 87% of the slot is untouched by every construction and gauge anchor. That says the payload has separate accessors and tells the next wake exactly what kind of code to look for, rather than reporting a thin map as a disappointment.

A NULL-CHECKED HEAD PLUS A PER-NODE BYTE TEST IS A LIST WALKER, AND ITS CALL SITES GIVE THE MODES. 0x0207871C reads [slot+0x558], returns on null, and tests node+0x40. Battle_Add calls it with r1 = 0 and r1 = 1 -- so the second argument is a mode, learned from the callers rather than the body.

ANCHOR DIVERSITY BOUNDS WHAT A FIELD MAP CAN SHOW. Twelve anchors drawn only from construction and gauge code produced twelve fields all in the same two bands. More anchors of the same kind would not have helped; the gap needs a different class of caller.

SIGNED AND HALFWORD LOADS HAVE 8-BIT OFFSETS, SO EVERY FIELD ABOVE +0xFF LOOKS SMALL IN A RAW SCAN. An ad-hoc scan of ComicDeck.cpp produced a tidy list of offsets 0xA0-0xFC that were ALL 0x500 too low. Only scans that resolve `add base,#N` then a small immediate report the truth -- and this ROM uses that form constantly.

TEST THE HYPOTHESIS THAT MOTIVATED THE WAKE, AND SAY WHEN IT FAILS. I opened expecting split bases to explain the empty +0x100..+0x557 band. Resolving them filled 0x5Cx instead. The band is genuinely untouched -- a stronger result than the guess would have been, but only because the guess got written down as refuted.

A CONDITIONAL EARLY RETURN NEEDS ITS OWN ANCHOR. `popne {r4,...,pc}` writes r4, so guard 2 correctly halted the walk two instructions before the SP field -- the most important field on the struct. Conservative guards do not fail loudly; budget an anchor after every conditional return in a function worth mapping.

THE MOST-ACCESSED FIELD IS USUALLY THE POINT OF THE STRUCT. +0x5C8 has 11 accesses against 1-5 for everything else, and it turned out to be the SP total. Sorting a field map by access count is a cheap way to find what a struct is FOR.

A REGION NO OFFSET SCAN TOUCHES MAY BE A LINKED STRUCTURE, NOT A MISSING MODULE. 0x500 bytes of the player slot showed nothing across three wakes of scanning because nothing ever computes `base + 0x58 + i*0x50` -- the nodes are linked onto a list at construction and reached only by traversal thereafter. Before hunting for the module that owns a silent region, check the constructor for a linking loop.

THE CONSTRUCTOR'S LINKING LOOP GIVES BASE, STRIDE, COUNT AND THE LIST HEAD AT ONCE. Nine instructions gave 16 x 0x50 at +0x58, the free-list head at +0x560, and the per-node initial value. Second time in four wakes that a construction loop outperformed every scan.

AN ARRAY THAT ENDS EXACTLY AT THE NEXT KNOWN FIELD IS SELF-CONFIRMING. 0x58 + 16*0x50 = 0x558, and +0x558 was already mapped independently as a list head. Arithmetic agreeing with a previously-established boundary is much stronger than arithmetic that merely divides evenly -- the lesson iteration 103 paid for with 0x645.

REFINE A WRONG READING RATHER THAN DEFENDING IT. Iteration 104 said the band has separate accessors; iteration 105 guessed split bases; both were wrong in different ways. Neither guess was load-bearing because each was recorded as a hypothesis, so replacing them cost nothing.

DISTINGUISH A PER-ITEM SKIP FROM A TRAVERSAL ABORT. node+0x40 skips one node; node+0x3C bit 0x2000 returns from the entire walk. Both look like `test, branch` in a loop body, and conflating them would invert what the flag means for every node after the first.

A ROUND-TOWARD-ZERO HALVING HAS A RECOGNISABLE SHAPE. `add r2,r2,r2,lsr #31` then `asr r2,r2,#1` is signed division by two, not a shift with a stray add. Reading it as two unrelated operations would have lost the only arithmetic relationship on the node.

MAP A SMALL RECORD FROM ITS INITIALISER PLUS ITS WALKERS. Two anchor classes -- the function that writes the fields and the functions that read them -- gave 20 of a 0x50-byte node. Constructors show the layout; walkers show which fields are live.

NAME THE MECHANISM, NOT THE MEANING, WHEN ONLY THE MECHANISM IS VISIBLE. The node has a flags word, a gated halving and a per-item skip. It is very tempting to call it a koma with a cost -- recorded as not claimed, because nothing in the code says so.

DISTINCT HIGH-BIT RETURN VALUES ARE A FUNCTION'S DOCUMENTATION. 0x10000000, 0x20000000 and 0x40000000 are three failure modes the author bothered to separate -- deck full, duplicate, and a validation failure. Reading only the success path would have missed the entire contract, and the error codes name the preconditions better than the code does.

A DUPLICATE CHECK NAMES A KEY. The add walks the active list comparing the first halfword of [node+0x34] against the requested id and refuses a match. That single loop establishes both that entries have IDs and that the collection is a set, not a bag.

SPLIT IMMEDIATES KEEP APPEARING -- `#0x158` THEN `#0x400` IS slot+0x558. Third distinct split form this campaign (add-then-access, ldrsb 8-bit offsets, and now two adds reaching a list head). Any offset scan that does not resolve them under-reports structure everywhere in this ROM.

READ A CONSTRUCTOR'S FAILURE PATHS FIRST. The three early returns took twelve instructions and gave the free-list head, the active-list head, the ID field, the uniqueness rule and two validator callees -- before reaching a single line of the fill.

A BOUNDS CHECK HANDS YOU THE TABLE'S ADDRESS, STRIDE AND LENGTH AT ONCE. 0x02076C98 is ten instructions and yields the ID table base, its 0xC-byte entry size and the field holding its count. Validators are the cheapest possible source of array geometry -- read them before any loop that walks the array.

ARGUMENT BOUNDS EXPLAIN PACKED FIELDS RETROACTIVELY. Iteration 108 saw two nibbles packed into node+0x0E with no idea of their range. `cmp #5` and `cmp #4` in the validator gave both, and confirmed the argument order. A packed field's width is a maximum, not its actual domain.

RE-VERIFY OLD GLOBAL LABELS WHEN NEW CODE TOUCHES THEM. 0x0214BD80 has sat in my notes as 'chr_b base ptr' for most of this campaign. One `str r0,[r3]` shows it holds the ComicDeck block. Labels inherited from early guesses survive precisely because nothing revisits them.

THE SAME FACT ARRIVING BY A SECOND ROUTE IS WORTH RECORDING. `mov r4,#4` beside `add r8,r0,#0x64` confirms four player slots independently of iteration 103's stride arithmetic. Cheap corroboration of a load-bearing number is worth the line it costs.

CHECK WHETHER A TABLE IS STATICALLY REACHABLE BEFORE PLANNING TO DUMP IT. Two queued table dumps have now died the same way: the base is a runtime pointer with no ROM-address store. The test is cheap -- look for a word store to the base offset within the owning module, and check whether it comes from a pc-literal or a call return.

A FAILED TASK CAN STILL PAY IF THE SEARCH TOUCHES THE RIGHT CODE. Hunting the table's base led through the add function again and settled node+0x34, which closed the entry-construction chain. Chasing the blocked thing was what surfaced the reachable thing beside it.

TWO FACTS THAT ONLY MAKE SENSE TOGETHER CORROBORATE EACH OTHER. The duplicate check reads [node+0x34]'s first halfword; node+0x34 is [deck+0x30] + id*0xC. Neither alone says table entries carry their id -- together they require it.

A VIRTUAL CALL IN AN INITIALISER MEANS THE DATA IS LOADED, NOT LINKED. `ldr r2,[r0]; ldr r2,[r2,#0x2c]; blx r2` feeding a table pointer is the signature of a resource fetch. Recognising it early would have saved the dump attempt.

FOURTH MASK BUG, SAME SIGNATURE -- THIS IS NOW A PROCESS FAILURE, NOT BAD LUCK. bl, ldr Rd/Rn, mov immediate, and now the pc-relative load: every time a mask and its compare value disagreed about which bits matter, and every time the result was a clean zero. The fix is not vigilance but a shared, tested helper for each encoding, so the mask is written once.

A DISTRIBUTION OF HOLDERS NAMES AN OBJECT'S OWNER BETTER THAN ANY SINGLE SITE. 37 of 55 holders in one overlay, and that overlay's allocation tags are all Koma*.cpp. Counting where a global is read tells you which subsystem the object belongs to -- cheaper than reading any of the functions.

A SINGLETON HOLDER IS AS INFORMATIVE AS A CLUSTER. Battle code touches the deck global exactly once, in the character-view path. That one site is the entire battle-to-deck interface, which is a much stronger statement than 'ov6 uses the deck'.

MODULE COMPANY IS EVIDENCE BUT NOT A SYMBOL. The 0x50 node lives in an object owned by an overlay full of Koma*.cpp files. That is worth recording and worth acting on, and it still is not the same as finding a string that names the record.

A TEST THAT ONLY CHECKS POSITIVE CASES CANNOT CATCH A MASK THAT MATCHES NOTHING. All four mask bugs this campaign produced empty results, so an assertion of the form 'this known instruction decodes correctly' would have passed every one only if the mask happened to be right. The rejection cases -- a conditional mov, a non-pc load, a bx -- are what make the new decoders trustworthy.

FIX THE PROCESS ON THE WAKE AFTER YOU NAME IT AS A PROCESS FAILURE. Iteration 111 called four mask bugs a process failure and queued a shared helper. Doing it immediately, before more engine work, is the only way that queue entry does not become the fifth bug's postmortem.

A memset AT CONSTRUCTION IS THE DEFAULT VALUE OF EVERY FIELD. Knowing the deck block is zeroed turns 'no writer found' from a weak negative into a concrete prediction -- the count is 0, so the bounds check rejects everything. The initial value is what makes an absent writer meaningful.

NAME THE EXACT SHAPE OF THE REMAINING DOUBT. 'No writer found' would be vague; '96 word stores to +0x30 in functions that do not load the global -- exactly what a callee taking the deck as an argument looks like' tells the next wake precisely what to attribute and why the current search missed it.

ENUMERATE THE ROUTES TO A POINTER, NOT THE WRITES TO AN OFFSET. Iteration 112 was stuck on 96 unattributed +0x30 stores. Listing the four ways any code can obtain a deck pointer -- the global in ARM, one call hop, the global in Thumb, and root+0x114 -- resolved all 96 at once: none of those routes writes the field, so none of the 96 can be the deck's. Second time this campaign that inverting the search closed a question the direct search could not.

A ZERO IN THE RIGHT PLACE IS STRONGER THAN A THOUSAND MATCHES ELSEWHERE. 375 Thumb stores at offset 0x30 exist, and they are all irrelevant because ZERO Thumb instructions load the deck global. One count made an entire instruction set drop out of the search.

STATE THE SCOPE OF A DEAD-CODE CLAIM IN THE CLAIM ITSELF. 'The deck's add-entry path is dead' invites 'but decks obviously work'. Saying it is the battle-side object, and naming the editor's separate allocations, keeps the finding from reading as absurd and stops a later wake from re-litigating it.

FIVE VESTIGIAL SYSTEMS IS NOW THE BASE RATE, NOT THE SURPRISE. ColPrm +0x68, +0xE8, +0x140, the view's 16-slot table, and now the deck add path. When a mechanism looks complete but its enabling field has no writer, that is the expected outcome in this build rather than a sign the search is wrong.

A RESIDUAL WORTH CLOSING IS ONE YOU CAN COUNT. 'Register-offset and stm stores are unswept' sounded open-ended until scoping it to the 72 functions that can hold the pointer produced 7 and 2 -- nine instructions, readable in one pass. Scope first, then decide whether the residual is expensive or trivial.

SHAPE DISTINGUISHES AN ARRAY WRITE FROM A FIELD WRITE. All seven register-offset stores index by a scaled register inside loops or bit-set idioms. A table base pointer is written once at a fixed offset. Recognising the idiom is faster and safer than tracing each base register to its origin.
`ldm rX!,{..}` FOLLOWED BY `stm rY!,{..}` IS AN INLINED memcpy. Two of the nine sites were a 32-byte block copy. Naming the idiom removes them from consideration without any base analysis.

CLOSING A RESIDUAL IS A LEGITIMATE WHOLE WAKE. Iteration 113's conclusion was already the interesting one; this wake added no new structure and made that conclusion unconditional. Leaving a named gap open indefinitely is how a strong finding quietly decays into a hedge.

ENUMERATE THE MUTATORS OF A CONTAINER, NOT ITS READERS. Six link/unlink sites decided the fate of two walkers, a remove function and every field they touch. Asking 'what can put something in here?' bounds a subsystem faster than reading anything that consumes it.

A DEAD FUNCTION'S REACH IS ITS DOWNSTREAM DATA, NOT JUST ITSELF. add-entry being dead was iteration 113's finding; that it is the SOLE producer for the active list makes four more functions dead. When something is proved unreachable, immediately ask what depended on its output.

AN ADD-PAIR SEARCH MUST ALLOW INTERVENING INSTRUCTIONS. My first sweep required the two `add`s to be adjacent and found zero sites -- including one I had already read by hand. Compilers interleave; the second add sat two instructions later behind a `mov r1,r4`.

A NEGATIVE ANSWER CAN BE THE ANSWER. 'How is the battle deck populated' had a clean resolution: it is not. Reporting that plainly is more useful than continuing to search for a population path that the mutation census shows cannot exist.

A THIRD SPLIT FORM: SCALED-REGISTER. `add rD, base, rI, lsl #2` then `[rD, #0x14]` is an array at +0x14, and the guarding `cmp r3,#6` gives its extent. Every split form found so far hides exactly the structural features worth having -- list heads, sub-regions, and now arrays. Assume any offset scan under-reports until each form is handled.

AN OPTIONAL ARGUMENT SHOWS AS PAIRED CONDITIONAL ARMS. `ldrne`/`strne` against `streq` around one `cmp r5,#0` says the source array may be null and the field is zeroed instead. Reading only the NE arm would have made the argument look mandatory.

A SHARED FACTORY IS A REASON NOT TO SPECIALISE A FINDING. 0x02026F94 builds the NoteTrack's +0x8C object and KomaList's +0x38. Noticing the repeat stops 'the KomaList's sub-object' becoming a deck-specific fact when it is engine infrastructure.

THE BUSIEST FIELD AND THE MODE FIELD ARE THE TWO WORTH READING NEXT. +0x04C and +0x3F0 tie at nine accesses; one is presumably state, the other selects behaviour. Access counts pick the reading order without any semantic guesswork.

TRUNCATING A TOOL'S OUTPUT CAN SILENTLY DROP A RESULT. Iteration 107's node table was short one field because `tail -20` on a 24-line scan cut the header and the first row. The scan was right; the reading was not. Use a bound larger than the expected output, or count the rows against the tool's own total.

A NEW GUARD'S FIRST DUTY IS TO EXPLAIN ITS OWN DELTA. The node map moving 20 -> 21 looked like guard 12 working. Checking the instruction showed a plain `str r3,[r4,#8]` and `scaled_array` returning None -- the guard had nothing to do with it. Attributing a change to the thing you just built is the easiest mistake to make and the cheapest to check.

CONDITIONAL EXECUTION IS THE NORM IN THIS ROM'S ARRAY CODE, NOT AN EDGE CASE. Guard 12's motivating example uses addne/addeq as the two arms of an optional copy. Every guard here that requires cond == AL is silently narrower than it looks -- worth re-auditing guards 8 and 9 for the same assumption.

AN UNCHANGED MAP IS A RESULT WORTH STATING. The ColPrm record and the battle character gained nothing from guard 12. Recording that as a genuine null result stops a later wake from suspecting the guard never ran on them.

RUNNING AN OLD TOOL WITH A NEWLY-LEARNED SIZE IS ITS OWN TASK. The ColPrm manager was mapped piecemeal across nine wakes because its size was unknown until iteration 101. One scanner run at 0xFB54 consolidated six scattered facts and added seven offsets. After learning a struct's size, re-run every tool that takes size as a parameter.

A GAP THAT MATCHES AN INDEPENDENTLY-DERIVED COUNT IS DESIGN, NOT A BUG. Nineteen stores in a twenty-slot span looked like an uninitialised dispatch slot until it matched iteration 62's 19-entry phase table exactly. Two derivations agreeing turns an alarming absence into a confirmed detail.

A GUARD FIX THAT CHANGES NOTHING IS STILL WORTH MAKING AND WORTH SAYING SO. Guard 8's AL requirement was the same latent narrowing guard 12 exposed. It had not yet cost a field -- recording that explicitly stops a future wake from wondering whether the relaxation silently altered earlier maps.

AN EXPECTED ABSENCE CONFIRMS THE MODEL. +0x154 missing from the constructor is exactly right if the accumulators own the contact array. Checking that a known field is NOT where it should not be is as informative as finding the ones that are.

A SPLIT IMMEDIATE'S LOW HALF LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE AN ADDRESS-TAKEN FIELD. +0x054, +0x254 and +0x354 all pair with a second add (0xC800, 0xDC00, 0xE000) to reach pool bases past 0xC000. Guard 8 cannot see the second add, so it reports three fields that do not exist. The tell is a guard-8 hit whose destination immediately feeds another add on itself.

PERFECT TILING IS THE STRONGEST FORM OF SIZE EVIDENCE. Three pools ending exactly at 0xFB54 with no gaps -- and each linking to a free-list head documented fifty wakes earlier -- confirms the layout, the counts, the node sizes and the allocation size simultaneously. Contrast iteration 103's 0x645, where exact division alone proved nothing because no code used the stride.

STATE WHICH NUMBERS WERE READ AND WHICH WERE DERIVED. The 0x80 and 0x200 counts come from `cmp` guards; the 80 for the middle pool comes from arithmetic between two pool bases. Both are sound here, but a later wake correcting one should not have to re-derive which was which.

A LARGE ALLOCATION IS USUALLY MOSTLY POOLS. 0xFB54 looked alarming for a manager until 0x1600 + 0x500 + 0x1800 of it turned out to be node storage. Check the tail of a big struct for tiling arrays before assuming the header is enormous.

A GUARD THAT REPORTS THE TRUE VALUE BEATS ONE THAT SUPPRESSES A FALSE ONE. I could have made guard 13 simply drop split-base hits. Reporting the accumulated offset instead turned three phantoms into four real pool bases, one of which (+0x454) revealed 128 embedded records. Suppression would have hidden the discovery along with the bug.

A SIZE CHECK CATCHES WHAT A DECODER CANNOT. The player slot's +0x21C became +0x61C, which equals the struct size and got flagged CONTAMINATED. Guard 13 has no way to know that value is a stride rather than a field -- the independent bound is what makes it safe.

AN EMBEDDED POOL EXPLAINS A FREE LIST WITH NO ALLOCATOR. Iteration 109 found a record free pool at manager+0x08 and no allocation to match it. The records are inline. When a pool has no allocator, look for its storage inside the owning object before assuming a missing writer.

CONFIRMING A SIZE FROM A SECOND, UNRELATED MECHANISM IS WORTH THE LINE. 0x188 came from the teardown's memset at iteration 77; it now also comes from the manager's construction stride. Two independent derivations of a load-bearing constant make every downstream field offset safer.

A FLAG SET AFTER A WIPE IS A FLAG THE WIPE WAS NOT MEANT TO CLEAR. The teardown does memset(record, 0, 0x188) and then immediately `orr #0x200` on +0x40. That ordering alone says the bit carries state the zeroed record still needs -- which is exactly what a free-list marker is.

THREE LIFECYCLE SITES PIN A FLAG'S MEANING WITHOUT READING ANY CONSUMER. Set at construction, cleared on acquire, set on release. No consumer of bit 0x200 was examined, and its meaning is not in doubt. Where a bit is WRITTEN across an object's lifetime can be more decisive than where it is read.

SEPARATE LOOPS FOR CLEARING AND LINKING IS THE NORM HERE, NOT AN ODDITY. Iteration 120 assumed one loop would do both and left the linking as an open question. The ColPrm manager uses one pass to zero records and another to link them -- as it also does for the bucket nodes. Look for a second pass before concluding a step is missing.

A COUNT CONFIRMED THREE INDEPENDENT WAYS IS WORTH THE REDUNDANCY. 128 records came from the clearing loop's bound, then the pool tiling, and now a `cmp` in the linking loop. Each derivation used different arithmetic, so the agreement is real evidence rather than one fact restated.

A REGION ABSENT FROM A CONSTRUCTOR IS NOT PART OF THE HEADER. Iteration 118 correctly predicted the contact array would be missing from a constructor map because the accumulators own it. Two wakes later I saw the same emptiness and filled it with 'header'. The earlier reasoning was right there in my own notes.

WHEN A SPAN SHOWS ZERO ACCESSES, ASK WHICH KNOWN STRUCTURE ENDS THERE. The gap ran to +0x453 and the records began at +0x454. One arithmetic check against an already-documented array closed it -- faster than any scan, and it needed no new evidence at all.

TILING THAT CLOSES EXACTLY IS WORTH RE-DERIVING AFTER EVERY CORRECTION. The manager's six spans now sum to 0xFB54 with no slack. Each earlier version also 'summed', because I was absorbing the unknown into a flexible header -- the sum only becomes evidence once every span has an independent source.

A NEGATIVE SCAN RESULT CAN CORROBORATE THE FIX RATHER THAN BLOCK IT. Finding zero accesses at +0x360..+0x453 among the manager's holders looked like a dead end. It is exactly what a computed-index array predicts, so it supports the contact-array reading instead of contradicting it.

PAIRING EACH `ldr rD,[pc]` WITH ITS FOLLOWING STORE RECOVERS A WHOLE POINTER TABLE IN ONE PASS. Nineteen phase handlers came out of forty-eight instructions with no per-slot reading. Any table filled from literals in a constructor yields to this, and the shared targets and no-ops fall out for free.

A FOUR-BYTE GAP BETWEEN TWO POINTER-TABLE TARGETS MEANS SINGLE-INSTRUCTION STUBS. 0x0207D9A4 and 0x0207D9A8 are four bytes apart, and both are `bx lr`. Spotting that in the recovered list pointed straight at the no-ops without disassembling all seventeen targets.

UPGRADE A DERIVED NUMBER TO A READ ONE WHEN THE CHANCE APPEARS. Iteration 119 got the 80-node count from arithmetic between two pool bases and said so. Passing the loop again while reading nearby fields turned it into a `cmp`. Recording the provenance is what made the upgrade visible as an improvement rather than a restatement.

WATCH THE EDIT PASS FOR DROPPED SPECIFICS, NOT JUST DROPPED HEX. The concision pass removed 'indices 0-3 sharing one' and '40 of 73' from a comparison, keeping the sentence but losing its substance. The token diff caught two bare integers going missing; without that check the claim would have survived as an unsupported assertion.

COUNTING UNIQUE ADDRESSES IN A POINTER TABLE ASSUMES ONE ADDRESS = ONE FUNCTION. Seventeen unique targets became '15 real handlers' in my write-up. Eight are interior entry points into two bodies and three are single-instruction stubs. Always resolve each target against the function database before describing a table's contents.

A SIZE OF 0 IN functions.json IS A SIGNAL, NOT MISSING DATA. Thirteen of the fifteen targets reported size 0 because they are not function starts. Reading that as 'the database is incomplete' rather than 'these are mid-function labels' would have inverted the finding.

A POINTER TABLE OF MOSTLY-TRIVIAL TARGETS IS AN INTERFACE, NOT A PIPELINE. Predicates returning a constant, a `mov r0,#0; bx lr`, and two `bx lr` stubs among 17 entries says the caller queries this object rather than driving stages through it. The two large bodies carry the actual work.

MY OWN SUMMARY LANGUAGE OUTRAN THE EVIDENCE BY ONE WAKE. Iteration 123's recovery of the 19 pointers was sound; only the word 'handlers' was unsupported. Correcting the description while keeping the data intact is cheaper than re-deriving, and worth doing the moment the gap is visible.

P125: a functions.json size can be RIGHT at the boundary and WRONG in granularity -- 0x0207DD40 size=540 ends exactly on a literal pool yet contains 8 bodies. Count `bx lr`/`pop {..,pc}` terminators inside a record before treating it as one function.

P125: pointer-table targets are exactly the case where a function detector merges bodies -- nothing branches between them, so only the table reveals the boundaries. Suspect every large record whose interior addresses appear in a table.

P125: `lsl #8` next to a comparison constant identifies the fixed-point scale, which converts opaque hex into a readable bound (0x3C000 -> 960). Look for the shift before guessing what a magic number means.
P125: two independent uses of the same constant (a test in one function, an emitted rect in another) is what upgrades `magic number` to `bound`. One use alone would not have.
P125: `mvn r0,#0x3bc00` = -(0x3C000-0x3FF) decided a struct layout question (signed extent, not second corner). A negative literal in a field is strong evidence that field is a delta.

P126: `addls pc, pc, rN, lsl #2` indexes from pc+8, i.e. the SECOND word after the addls. The branch immediately following it is the out-of-range default, not case 0. I read the list positionally last wake and shifted every case by one. Always write out the pc+8 arithmetic before assigning case indices.

P126: a wrong-but-plausible case map produced a confident published claim ('cases 2,3,4,5 share one target') that no gate caught, because every address in it was real. Address-level checks cannot catch index-level errors -- only re-deriving the arithmetic can.

P126: functions.json is INCONSISTENT here, not uniformly wrong -- 0x0207DFD8 is listed at exactly the right size while its three neighbours are missing and 0x0207DFF4 is merged. Do not infer a blanket rule about the database from one bad record; check each.

P126: two functions independently agreeing on the meaning of a value (r1 in {1,2} tested here, emitted as wall rects by the getter) is the same corroboration pattern that upgraded the arena bounds in P125. Look for the second, independent use.

P126: near-duplicate functions differing only in WHICH argument register holds the out pointer (r2 vs r3) prove a pointer table is not one uniform virtual interface. Do not assume a shared signature across slots.

P127: when two arms branch oppositely on one callee's result, read the CALLEE FIRST. Four instructions with no branch settled instantly that the asymmetry had to be in the callers -- I could have skipped two wakes of speculation.
P127: an asymmetry seen once is ambiguous; seen twice in independent functions it is an idiom. The 0x0207F410/0x0207F448 pair converted 'bug or design?' into 'design' with no new tooling.

P127: how callers CONSUME a return value bounds its type even when the writers are unfindable. Every one of 21 sites compares to 0, so a ldrb that could carry 0-255 is a boolean in practice -- a real claim that costs nothing.
P127: resist upgrading a good story to a finding. 'Side/team selector' fits the two-object comparison AND the opposite walls, but nothing names it, so it stays SPECULATIVE.

P127: +0x48 joins +0x08/+0x10/+0x18/+0x20 on the conventional-offset list (644 hits, 18 strb). Check the hit count BEFORE planning a field-writer hunt -- it decides whether the hunt is a task or a dead end.

P128: to tell a vtable slot's DIRECTION (getter vs setter), find a call site where the argument was computed from somewhere ELSE and guarded by a changed-check. Iteration 127 saw the same slot called with a freshly-read value and could not tell; one better call site settled it.
P128: what the code DOES in response to a flag change identifies the flag better than any of its readers. 21 readers only proved it was a boolean; one in-place negation made it a facing bit.

P128: a redundant `moveq r0,#0` after `cmp r0,#0` is the compiler materialising a ternary's NULL branch -- it means the guard PRODUCES the null rather than skipping the call. Do not read a compare-against-zero as a guard without checking where control actually goes.
P128: reading a 16-byte and a 40-byte helper cost almost nothing and converted the tail of the caller from opaque to exact. Read the tiny callees before theorising about the caller.
P128: prefer between two rival readings by their DISCRIMINATOR, and say what it is. 'Facing beats team because the response is a geometric mirror' is checkable; 'facing fits better' is not.

P129: one more hop can upgrade an inference without new evidence about the inference itself -- learning +0x0C was one axis of THREE turned P128's 'negated a coordinate' into 'single-axis mirror', which is much better support for 'facing'.

P129: spend the one command to verify an argument order when the two readings differ in KIND. memcpy(dst,src) made 0x02024BE4 a reset; the reverse would have made it a set-from-caller. Rival readings that differ in kind justify the detour; ones that differ in detail do not.

P129: a re-read of a field after a callback (0x02024C64 reloading +0x24 instead of reusing r2) is evidence about the CALLBACK -- it says the handler is allowed to modify that field. Redundant-looking loads carry information.

P129: bits set OUTSIDE a transition test are a deliberate design signal, not sloppiness. 0x30 is or'd in after the cmp, so those two bits never notify -- worth recording as a property of the flag scheme.
P129: the merged-record hazard now spans 540 bytes (P125), 36 bytes (P126) and ONE instruction (P129). Size is no guide to whether a record is merged; check the terminator every time.

P130: when a task fails, MEASURE why and publish the measurement. '3 accesses near the setter, all inside it; 64 unattributed candidates' turns a dead end into a scoped next task; 'I could not find it' would not.

P130: the census answers RANGE questions, not just size questions. Sorting its sites by address instead of size produced the library/game boundary -- a structural fact about the binary from a tool I had been using for one purpose only.

P130: 0x0206ADB8 is the boundary. Every nameless helper this investigation leaned on (memcpy, memset, list link/unlink, 0x02024C3C, 0x02024BE4, 0x02011B38) is below it. Do not spend another wake trying to name sub-0x0206ADB8 functions from tags -- there are none by construction.
P130: two allocation sites sharing a FILE tag AND a SIZE pin a class size by call-site binding, which is much stronger than the nearest-symbol heuristic. Look for create/clone pairs.
P130: bracketed containment (between two sites naming the same file) beats nearest-neighbour proximity but is still proximity -- a .cpp boundary can fall in the gap. Keep it PLAUSIBLE.
P130: `lsl #N; lsr #0x1f` is the compiler's single-bit test. Decode it as bit (31-N) rather than skipping it as shift noise -- it names a flag bit for free.

P131: a repeated-argument value is identifiable by looking at MULTIPLE sites in ONE function. Five allocations in CommonHSV_Create settled 'tag vs __LINE__' instantly: tags repeat, line numbers increase and come in adjacent pairs. One site alone could never have shown it.

P131: I had used alloc_census.py for ~30 wakes while its own docstring mis-described argument 4. Tool documentation is a claim like any other and deserves the same evidence standard -- re-derive it when a cheap test exists.

P131: a C++ copy-constructor chain is a free class hierarchy AND a free member map. Each level calls its base, overwrites the vptr at +0x00, then copies exactly its own members -- so reading one clone function upward names every level and its fields.

P131: an ARM immediate that is not encodable gets built by arithmetic on a register that already holds a nearby value (add r3, r0, #0xf1 for 0x111). Treat COMPUTED in a census as 'the compiler was clever here', not 'the tool failed'.

P131: dumping the constants (vtable addresses, counter globals) at the moment they appear turns a structural finding into follow-up tasks with concrete addresses. 0x0209C30C and 0x0209E114 now make the P127-P129 vtable slot offsets resolvable.

P132: DIFF a derived vtable against its parent, then look the differing entries up in the census. That named slot +0x18 as Clone without disassembling one instruction of it -- the cheapest naming route found so far.
P132: 41 of 44 identical slots is not noise, it IS the finding -- it proves the two tables are parent/child and isolates the override set to three slots. Sameness can be the evidence.
P132: an ODD function pointer in a vtable means a Thumb target. Do not treat it as a corrupt word; subtract 1.

P132: my own inferred LABELS are the weakest links in the chain and the ones to attack first. 'Notify' for vtable +0x18 came from call position, never from reading the target, and it now conflicts with hard evidence. Label slots by offset until the target is read.

P132: a stale lead can be revived by a later structural fact rather than new searching -- P130's untraced bit-0x40 site resolved the moment I knew 0x02021960 was this family's base copy ctor. Re-check parked leads after every hierarchy discovery.

P132: the token diff caught a benign edit (a repeated +0x18 replaced by 'that slot'). Verify what the guard flags rather than trusting or dismissing it -- both a real drop and a stylistic one look identical in the count.

P133: I used 0x0201A21C as 'the allocator' for ~100 iterations without ever disassembling it. It is 12 bytes and a veneer. Read the thing you cite, however obvious it seems -- especially a foundation every other finding rests on.
P133: `ldr ip,[pc]; bx ip; .word target` is a linker long-branch veneer. Recognise it before attributing behaviour to the address; the semantics live at the target.

P133: a wrong runtime model can coexist with correct findings. The tags are discarded at runtime, yet every census name is still valid -- because the evidence was the CALL SITE, not the callee. Know which end of a call your evidence comes from.
P133: allocation SIZES from two different levels of a hierarchy cross-check a member offset for free. 0x80 (parent clone) + a halfword at +0x80 = 0x84 (derived clone), all read independently.

P133: the C++ ABI gives away the first two vtable slots -- two near-identical bodies where the second adds a free call are the destructor and the deleting destructor. Look for that pair at +0x00/+0x04 in any vtable.

P133: a mis-identified helper can hide a whole second code path. Because 0x0201A21C looked like the allocator, the census never scanned 0x0201A228 -- a blind spot that existed for ~100 iterations and is invisible until you read the veneer.
P133: the mandatory edit pass timed out at 120s on an 8KB doc. Verify the file is unchanged before retrying, and allow ~420s -- a partial in-place edit would be far worse than a slow one.

P134: a guard written for one code path is not a guard. The Thumb pass bounded implausible sizes from iteration 101; the ARM pass never did, and nothing revealed it until a new scan reached code that tripped it. When adding a guard, ask which other passes need the same one.

P134: after widening a scan, DIFF the old output against the corresponding subset of the new. '659 old rows vs 659 new veneer rows, diff empty' proves the change was additive -- far stronger than re-running a selftest that only checks anchors.

P134: printing an unresolved address in a column headed 'file' reads as data even when the tool is being honest about not knowing. Suppress it and say UNTAGGED, but pair the suppression with an assertion that fires if real data ever shows up there.

P134: answering an explicitly-parked 'not claimed' question is worth a whole wake. P133 asked whether tagged calls reach the allocator directly; the answer (0 of 403) turned a caveat into a clean structural fact.

P134: the stale-register false positive recurs across every register the back-scanner resolves -- sizes (P101), Thumb names, and now r1/r2 at untagged sites. Assume any register the caller did not visibly set holds garbage.

P135: a negative result is worth publishing when it BOUNDS something. 'Largest direct allocation is 0xE4' retires the whole idea that big structures were hiding behind the untagged entry, and it took one sweep.

P135: distinguish a tool change that adds COVERAGE from one that adds REACH. P134 added 403 sites and zero new large objects; saying so stops a future wake from re-mining the same seam expecting managers.

P135: the best validation of a widened scan is that it independently rediscovers something found by a DIFFERENT method. The sweep hit 0x0204B0D4, which P133 reached via a vtable diff -- stronger evidence than any selftest anchor.
P135: an allocation SIZE is a class fingerprint. Grouping census sites by size found seven callers of one 0x80 class immediately, which is a cheaper way into a class family than following pointers.
P135: when one size has several distinct constructors, do not choose between 'overloads' and 'sibling classes' without the vtable store at +0x00. Both explain the shape equally well.

P136: I drifted nine wakes from Mission 2 into middleware, each step locally reasonable. Re-read the mission when several consecutive wakes share no addresses with the mission's own subsystems -- that is the drift signal.

P136: a queue entry naming an ALLOCATION SITE is not naming the function. 'Battle_MoveManCreate 0x02082A50' was wrong in a dozen docs; the function starts 0x18 earlier. Resolve a site to its function before quoting it as an entry point.

P136: when a reading is surprising (a memset undoing the initialisation before it), check the three things that could make it wrong -- the literal's value, whether any branch skips it, whether the register was rewritten -- before publishing. All three held here.
P136: DEAD code is still a layout document. The wiped loop gave 128 records of 0xC at +0x48, which nothing in the surviving code reveals.

P136: finding the same six-step construction block in two managers reached from opposite directions corroborates BOTH readings at once. Recognising a shape already documented is worth more than a new one-off.
P136: 'the null check jumps into shared cleanup instead of returning' is now confirmed twice (P128, P136). Treat it as this codebase's habit and expect NULL-deref-on-OOM rather than graceful failure.

P137: zero writers for a high offset may mean the offset is not a FIELD at all. 0x648 was only ever a loop bound, and it is not an encodable ARM immediate -- so both the empty scan and the split-add in the constructor were expected, not anomalies.

P137: before trusting a perfect tiling, name what is missing. 0x648 + 128*0x40 = 0x2648 exactly, elements need >=0x38, and 0x40 is the only aligned stride that fits -- yet no instruction computes base + i*0x40, so it stays PLAUSIBLE. Say which observation would upgrade it.

P137: when offset scanning comes back empty, read the tool's own blind-spot list and pick the one that fits. 'A pointer to a sub-region passed as an argument' was the answer, and the consumer confirmed it in one instruction (ldr lr,[ip,#8]).

P137: a 0xC record IS the list link in this codebase (next/prev/payload). A constructor zeroing +0x8 of N records is initialising N payload pointers -- which also tells you N elements exist somewhere else.

P137: `dst = src` pairs at adjacent offsets (+0x14 <- +0x0C, +0x18 <- +0x10) are a previous/current snapshot for delta computation. A flag that skips the copy for one pass marks a newly created or teleported element.

P137: read a big loop's HEAD and TAIL first. The tail gave the iteration form (linked list, not array) and the head gave the element layout; the ~180 instructions in between were not needed for either.

P138: the companion pass is what makes a 1092-hit offset tractable. Three writes to +0x34 in ONE function with all four companion offsets present picked the right candidate out of 85 direct writers immediately.

P138: a failed hunt still narrows the target if you say WHY the obvious place was wrong. The allocator snapshots on every branch, so a fresh element never needs the suppressor -- which redirects 0x100 toward repositioning rather than closing the question.

P138: the cheapest way to strengthen a size hypothesis is to find the HIGHEST touched offset. +0x3E moved the element from >=0x38 to >=0x3F, leaving 0x40 as the only aligned fit that also tiles. Look for the deepest field before hunting for a stride computation.

P138: the SAME initialisation snippet appearing three times in one function (once per branch) is proof of shared type with another function that does it once -- a compiler will not duplicate an unrelated pattern that precisely.

P138: an offset matching a queued question is not an answer to it. [installer_arg0+0xF0] shares a number with the queued ColPrmMan+0xF0 item, and I have no evidence the two bases are the same object. Same offset, different claim.
P138: when two readings of a pointer both fit, name the single observation that would separate them (here, what arg1 is at the call site) rather than picking the more attractive one.

P139: reasoning from a recognisable CONSTANT is weaker than reading where the data comes from. 0x10000 being a famous 16.16 `1.0` sent me to 'scale pair'; one read of the caller showed +0x0C/+0x10 are positions and the 0x10000 is a default position.
P139: when a value's meaning is uncertain, the caller that supplies it is usually one read away. Prefer chasing the source over interpreting the bit pattern.

P139: I predicted this read would settle P137's ambiguity and it did not. Record the failed prediction next to the finding -- otherwise the ambiguity quietly looks resolved because a wake was spent on it.

P139: two functions touching the same offsets are not necessarily on the same list. The consumer reaches its list via [[[arg0+4]+0x10]+0x10] while the allocator links onto container+0x00 -- different chains, so shared offsets prove nothing about shared structure.
P139: a third independent sighting of the same pointer chain ([[owner+4]+0x50]) is worth noting explicitly. Repeated arrival at one object from unrelated modules is how a structure earns confidence.
P140: to prove a stack slot is dead, grep the WHOLE function for loads from it rather than reading forward until you get bored. One scan of 111 instructions settled what P139 had guessed wrong about.

P140: a call can be dead code too. 0x0201899C's buffer is overwritten and its return value clobbered, so the call contributes nothing -- I had been treating 'there is a bl' as evidence that something happens.

P140: read a constructor for what it stores from its ARGUMENTS, not just what it stores. record+0x34/+0x38 had been known as fields the allocator reads since iteration 70; the installer named their source in two instructions.

P140: one argument feeding two fields in different encodings (arg2 stored whole at +0x34, its low nibble re-encoded into +0x3C bits 4-7 with a 0x400000 marker) means naming that argument pays twice. Prioritise arguments that appear more than once.

P140: a split immediate (add #0x100 then offset +0x86) is the signature of an offset above 0xFFF or otherwise unencodable -- the same mechanism that hid +0x648 in P137. Expect it for every field past +0xFF in a large struct.
P140: two stores to the same offset back to back (strb r7 then strb r2 at record+0x175) is a dead store. Note it; do not silently report only the surviving value.

P141: verify argument numbering with FRAME ARITHMETIC before building on it. Pushed-register count plus the sub tells you exactly where a caller's [sp+0] lands; two frames agreeing with the offsets each function reads is cheap proof.

P141: a field's meaning comes from the VALUES real callers pass, not from its writer. record+0x38 had been a named field for 70 wakes; four call sites gave it a shape (zero or one bit = a category mask) in one read.
P141: single-bit constants spread across 0x800/0x4000/0x8000 rule out a size or an index. The distribution of observed values is itself the evidence for 'mask'.

P141: when every visible caller zeroes the input a branch depends on -- one site even doing bic r2,r3,#0xf deliberately -- say 'no observed live caller' and name the untraced path, rather than either claiming it dead or ignoring it.

P141: a thin wrapper that injects a default (0x02083624 forcing arg3=0) means the subsystem has two entry points, and callers of the wrapper will never exercise whatever that argument controls. Check for wrappers before concluding an argument is always set.

P141: I mistyped the installer's branch addresses as 0x02083A.. in my own draft and caught it by re-disassembling before the edit pass. Re-verify addresses transcribed from an earlier wake's notes rather than from a fresh read.

P142: the strongest confirmation is writer values and reader tests agreeing from opposite ends of a chain. Callers writing 0x4000/0x8000 plus consumers tst-ing 0x4000/0x8000 settled in one read what four call sites alone left PLAUSIBLE.
P142: `tst` versus `cmp` is the discriminator between a bitmask and a number. Every consumer using tst is itself the evidence -- no need to find a definition.
P142: a field can be one of TWO independent gates on the same operation. Here direction flags and the category mask both have to pass; reading only one of them would have produced a half-right story.
P142: `lsl #7` next to a `lsl #8` base is not a different format, it is HALF. Compare shift amounts within one expression before reaching for a fixed-point interpretation.

P142: adjacent offsets with overlapping bit values are a trap worth recording explicitly. fp at +0x44 uses 0x100/0x200 just like the record's +0x40 flags, on a different base and with different meanings -- I wrote down that they must not be merged.
P142: when two of three observed values for a field are explained, say which one is not. 0x800 has a writer and no reader, and naming that gap is what makes it the next task.

P143: filter a common-immediate search by the instruction that must PRECEDE it. 13 `tst #0x800` candidates became 3 by requiring a `+0x38` load one instruction earlier -- most of the rest were a different field's flags at +0x40.
P143: a bit tested on BOTH participants of a pair, where either one vetoes, is a different kind of flag from one tested on a single object. Note which side of an interaction a flag is read from.

P143: do not force one meaning onto a bit whose polarity differs between sites. Set means 'branch away' at one site and 'proceed' at another; both are recorded, neither is reconciled, because iteration 127 showed what labelling an asymmetry early costs.

P143: one field can mix categories of bit. +0x38 holds axis selectors AND behavioural control, so 'it is a layer mask' was too tidy -- check each new bit's role rather than extending the field's label to it.

P143: `tst rX, rY` (register against register) is the shape of a mask-against-mask test and would be a major find, but operands set outside the read window must stay untraced. Name the shape, withhold the claim.

P144: my top-ranked lead was wrong, and two instructions showed it. `tst rX, rY` looks like mask-against-mask, but one operand was a pc-relative LITERAL. Check where BOTH operands come from before naming the shape of a test.
P144: a mask constant that omits exactly the bit the known callers set is a real finding, not an error to smooth over. 0x6FF excludes 0x100; say so precisely and let the puzzle stand.

P144: before claiming a field is unaccounted, grep the prior findings for that offset. I drafted +0xB0 as a gap in the 'fully accounted' manager layout; it was already recorded as bucket 17, and the check turned a false refutation into a sharper claim (the bucket index is hardcoded).

P144: a second writer is enough to block a runtime conclusion. Construction-time values gave a tempting story about exclusion; 0x0207EF1C writing +0x34 means the value at test time is undetermined, so the claim stays narrow.
P144: a constant `add rD, base, #imm` into a list-head array means a HARDCODED index. Compute which element it is (0x28 + N*8 here) rather than treating the offset as an opaque field.

P145: I trusted a scan's reported base register without tracing it, and built a P144 claim on it. The scan says `base=r2`; r2 was loaded from [r4+0x5C] two instructions earlier. ALWAYS trace the base before attributing a store to a struct.

P145: two different objects had a flags word at the SAME offset +0x34, which is exactly how the misattribution slipped through. When an offset is on the conventional list, the base is the only thing that identifies the struct.

P145: an inference about why a function would NOT need a flag pointed straight at the answer. Iteration 138 reasoned 'the allocator snapshots on every branch, so it does not need the suppressor -- therefore repositioning does' and iteration 145 found exactly that. Negative reasoning about the wrong candidate is a real search technique.

P145: retracting a reason is not the same as retracting a conclusion. P144's withheld runtime claim was right for a different reason (85 untraced writers), so I corrected the reason and left the conclusion standing.
