P145: `smlabb rD, rIdx, rStride, rBase` is an indexed table access -- decode it as base + index*stride rather than skipping it as a multiply. Here it exposed a 0x18-stride table that drives element flags from data.

P146: an apparent contradiction in a flag's polarity usually means one of the two branch TARGETS is misread. Reading both targets turned 'opposite meanings' into 'include here, exclude there' -- ordinary routing.

P146: a withheld conclusion can be resolved by finding the writer you suspected existed. P144 declined to claim exclusion because a second writer might exist; there is one, and it ORs exactly the bits the reader tests.

P146: verify subagent claims against the disassembly before publishing. One reported 2 callers where query.py lists one caller twice (an edge plus its bl site) and 'corrected' a note of mine that was right.

P146: Codex is well suited to self-contained encoding/arithmetic checks -- give it raw instruction words, not addresses, so it decodes independently. It confirmed 7 claims and correctly split evidence I had conflated: tiling proves the REGION's record size, a field offset proves only a MINIMUM for THAT struct.
P146: when a misattribution is found, look for siblings. The retracted +0x5C store was one of seven instances of the same base-confusion shape on the same offset.

P146: a cited corroborating artifact that does not exist is itself evidence. Asked to rewrite the charter on the strength of docs/PROJECT-GOAL.md, I checked -- the file is absent from every branch -- so the charter edit stays with the owner.

P146b: a rule-preservation check must be whitespace-insensitive. My line-based grep reported the one-task-per-wake rule as MISSING after the edit pass; it had merely wrapped across two lines. Flatten whitespace before counting, or a reflow reads as a deletion.

P146b: when an edit pass touches a doc containing OPERATING RULES rather than findings, diff the rules explicitly by name -- the numeric-token diff only guards addresses and counts, and would not have noticed a reworded constraint.

P146c: a runtime index that divides with NO REMAINDER validates a base and a stride simultaneously. (0xAC8-0x648)/0x40 = 18 exactly; a wrong base or stride would almost certainly not divide evenly. One measurement, two claims.

P146c: before asking the runtime side to sweep inputs, check whether the address is even on the path. The three entity-constructor call sites sit in map-item and object-control code, so an attack-input sweep against them could only ever return zero -- which is exactly what 06 measured.
P146c: census-named neighbours bracketing an unnamed function is enough to redirect a search, but not enough to claim the function's module. Kept as PLAUSIBLE while still acting on it.

P146c: the partner session's empirical zeros corroborated two of my static findings for free -- the destructor memset showed up as elements reading back zero, and the stack-temp xy argument showed up as a DTCM pointer. Ask for field dumps even when the fields are expected to be empty.

P147: a function's identity can be read straight off the allocator's __FILE__/__FUNCTION__ args at the call site -- the strongest attribution available under static-only rules, and stronger than the module-range proximity the projectile section had been relying on. Look for it before reaching for ranges.

P147: a dispatch table's arity can be pinned without any bound check in the code -- the next data object after it (here the "BattleObjShot.cpp" string at 0x021728D0) is the upper bound. 0x02172864..0x021728CF = 0x6C = 27 entries exactly.

P147b: reciprocity with the runtime validator paid off immediately -- checking that my own requested address was actually on the path turned up a bigger result than the sweep would have, plus a tool blind spot. Verify reachability BEFORE asking for a run, every time.

P147b: before writing 'first time X is named', grep the findings dir for X. I re-derived findings/thumb-caller-audit.md's whole result and briefly published it as novel. The 145-file findings dir is a searchable prior-art index -- use it as one BEFORE claiming novelty, not after.

P147b: a tool's strict mode can be quietly stricter than its targeted mode. find_thumb_callers.py --audit gates on a plausibility heuristic that --to skips, so --audit's census is a floor. When a broad audit and a targeted query disagree, read the filter -- don't average them.

P147c: an uncredentialed external lead (a 2007 community guide) is still useful as a place to point the disassembler -- but check whether the CODE SEMANTICS match the mechanic, not just the data shape. record+0x34's nibble has exactly the attacker-vs-target shape a per-move nature needs, and still almost certainly isn't one, because it excludes targets rather than scaling damage.

P148: a heuristic that gates a CENSUS converts absence of evidence into a reported number. find_thumb_callers.py's 187 read as a count and was a floor. When a tool reports a total, check whether anything is dropped before the total is computed -- and make it print a floor and a ceiling instead of one number.

P148: two windows in the same predicate should match unless there's a reason. The +/-2 adjacent-call window next to a +/-8 marker window was almost certainly an oversight, and it cost roughly half the audit's hits.

P149: encoding arithmetic can CLOSE a blind spot instead of merely bounding it. owner+0xE8 cannot be written by any direct Thumb immediate store because 0xE8 > 0x7C, the ARMv4T STR imm5 ceiling -- so the Thumb gap strengthens B11 rather than threatening it. Check expressibility before scanning.

P149: sort 'vestigial' claims by what the claim is MADE OF before re-auditing them. Of seven, three were not reachability-or-writer claims at all (written-never-read inside one function, overwritten by a memset, explicitly-not-a-claim). A blind spot in the call/store graph cannot touch those.

P149: asking the independent checker BEFORE forming a conclusion caught an error forming a conclusion first would have hidden -- I mis-transcribed a halfword (0x6668 for 0x66bc) and it flagged the inconsistency rather than decoding around it. Owner's inverted order is better; adopt it for load-bearing decodes.

P149: a checker working in a different coordinate system than you is worth more than one that agrees in your own. Codex read a BL as a relative displacement (A+0xD40) with no address context; query.py reads absolute (0x0215305C). Their agreement validated where the bytes came from, which neither tool could establish alone. Prefer checks that differ in representation, not just in operator.

P150: when a peer's runtime result and my static map disagree on what an ADDRESS IS, check the address before accepting either framing. 0x0215D3B4 was reported as a vtable and is a 300-byte ARM function with a push prologue. Separate a peer's MEASUREMENT from their LABELLING -- the first can be solid while the second is wrong.

P150: a contradiction in my own state may be an artefact of how evidence was COLLECTED, not a fact about the code. The ov05 conflict sat unresolved for many iterations; the likely cause is a residency measurement taken on a misidentified screen because the boot nav was wrong. Before hunting code to explain a contradiction, ask whether the measurement measured what it claimed to.

P150: a closure that holds under EVERY value of an unresolved variable beats resolving the variable. deck+0x30's last candidate stores zero, and the claim needs the field to stay zero -- so r5's identity stopped mattering. Look for the argument that makes the open question irrelevant before spending a wake closing it.

P150: incoherent instruction PAIRS are a decoder-bug detector. 'mov' immediately before 'beq' cannot be right because mov sets no flags. Read for semantic coherence across adjacent instructions, not just per-instruction plausibility -- that is what caught cmp-decoded-as-mov.

P150: convergent verification earned its place in the charter on first real use. Three decodes agreed on the load-bearing instruction (so the deck result is solid) and two-of-three disagreed with the project tool on 0x2800, which localised the defect. Agreement confirmed the claim; disagreement found the bug.

P151: the blast radius of a decoder bug is not where the bad instructions are, it is where CONTROL FLOW conclusions were drawn. All three flagged CITED addresses turned out to be literal-pool data and harmless; the real damage was nine uncited instructions, three of which were the guards that made a three-way selection look like one path with dead tails.

P151: checking cited addresses is necessary but not sufficient when auditing a tool bug. Scan the whole CODE RANGE a doc reasons over, not just the addresses it happened to quote -- the quoted ones were fine and the unquoted ones carried the error.

P152: an implausibly large number is itself evidence of a measurement bug. 97.3% missing would have meant the database did not work at all, which contradicts using it successfully every wake. Sanity-check a scary statistic against lived experience of the tool BEFORE writing it down.

P152: 'inside a function extent' needs to mean the ENCLOSING function, not any function. Comparing against any-extent gave 97.3%; comparing against the enclosing one gave 71% of a 9.4% missing set -- a real and actionable pattern instead of noise.

P152: a predicate can be consulted at more than one level of the same decision. 0x0208C51C gates whether Path B is chosen AND gates the branch inside both of Path B's functions. Do not assume one test per decision point when reading a selection tree.

P153: WHERE a global is referenced from can identify it when nothing names it. 0x0214CCF8 has no string and no alloc tag, but being touched 245 times from ONLY the local-wireless and online overlays -- and zero times from arm9 -- pins it to networking. Reference-provenance is evidence; use it when symbol evidence is absent.

P153: a 24-byte function with 47 callers is a design signal, not a curiosity. It meant arm9 needed to ask an overlay-owned question without linking the overlay, which is why the state lives in a fixed RAM slot below the overlay load base. Odd caller-count-to-size ratios point at architecture.

P153: running the raw scan ALONGSIDE the database query (not instead of it) is now paying off every time. Here the DB gave 4 and the truth was 9, on the one global the whole finding rested on. With a measured 9.4% index gap, never let a DB count be the last word on a load-bearing question.

P154: check heap-vs-static BEFORE reaching for the allocation census. 0x021AA0D8 is static RAM between two overlay images, so it has no allocator call site and therefore no tag -- the census hypothesis I queued was unfalsifiable by construction, not merely unproductive. A tool that works by attributing call sites cannot see objects that were never allocated.

P154: some confidence labels have a CEILING set by the evidence type, not by how much evidence accumulates. The networking reading now has address, size, init, teardown and overlay provenance and still cannot exceed PLAUSIBLE, because static allocation guarantees no symbol will ever name it. Say so explicitly instead of implying more evidence would promote it.

P154: state a scan's limitation BEFORE presenting its numbers, not in a footnote. My offset histogram does not track register liveness, and the largest offsets it reports are exactly where that flaw would show. Presenting the +0xC40 figures without the caveat would have invited a wrong structural claim about overlay RAM reuse.

P155: a scan whose interesting answer is 'nothing survived' MUST have a positive control, or a broken scan is indistinguishable from a clean negative. My suspicion about the naive histogram happened to be correct, so a silently-empty tool would have 'confirmed' it and I would have published a right conclusion for a wrong reason.

P155: never pick a binary by sorted(glob(...))[0]. sorted() put arm7.bin ahead of arm9.bin and the tool silently scanned the wrong CPU's image. My earlier ad-hoc scans were correct only by luck of unsorted directory order. Name the file.

P155: hedging the SUSPICIOUS part of a result is not enough -- I flagged P154's large offsets and let the small ones pass, and the small ones were equally bogus. When a method is unsound, distrust ALL of its output, not just the implausible-looking tail.

P156: a peer's hypothesis can be TRUE and still not explain what it was offered to explain. The 0x0214E480 overlay-aliasing fact is real and confirmed, but the campaign's damage conclusion never depended on that address. Check whether a proposed explanation is load-bearing before accepting or rebuilding on it.

P156: asking the independent checker with NO hypothesis produced a cold-start corroboration worth more than agreement would have been. It reconstructed the two-nibble layout, the +0x12 destination and the sentinel role of 3 from bytes alone -- sharing no reasoning with the original finding -- and incidentally caught a 'copy' that was not a copy.

P156: 'we happened to label it right' is a near-miss, not a save. No rule required checking overlay aliasing for addresses in the 0x0214CD20 window before reasoning about them in a battle context; correct labelling was habit. Turn near-misses into rules.

record_0x34_nibble.CONFIRMED_STATIC: 0x0216A944 arm A computes a 4-bit value from the ATTACKER's record+0x34 low nibble (merging the 0xF0 nibble via lsr #4 when attacker's +0x38 has 0x800) and tests it against each TARGET's record: skip if target +0x38 & 0x800; skip if (r5 tst target+0x3C & 0xF); skip if target+0x17C == 0 OR attacker nibble == target nibble.
record_0x34_nibble.two_fields: record+0x34's low BYTE holds two 4-bit fields, not one -- the 0xF0 nibble is conditionally folded into the low nibble.
record_0x34_nibble.dual_use: the same r5 is used as a bitmask (tst against +0x3C&0xF) AND as an equality operand (cmpne against target nibble) -- constrains it to a small bitfield where equal means same single bit.
record_0x34_nibble.PLAUSIBLE: team/side filter -- don't spawn onto your own side. Matching values EXCLUDE the target.
record_0x34_nibble.not_claimed: per-move attack nature. justoolkit-47 relayed a 2007 GameFAQs guide claim that each move has its own Attack Nature. The shape here (attacker value vs target fields) is what that needs, but the SEMANTICS argue against it: a nature-vs-nature rule would SCALE DAMAGE, not delete the target from the spawn set. This is spawn selection, before any damage arithmetic. If a per-move nature field exists, look at a damage-scaling site, not here.

THUMB_STORE_TRIAGE.why: find_field_writers.py declares 'Thumb code -- ARM-mode functions only' as a blind spot, so every no-writer claim rested on an ARM-only store scan. P149 asks which of the seven vestigial claims that can actually reach.
THUMB_STORE_TRIAGE.exposed: only record+0x68 and deck+0x30 (partly). Three of the seven are not reachability/writer claims at all (installer dead buffer = written-never-read in one ARM fn; MovMan dead init = overwritten by memset; shared decoders = explicitly not a claim). View handler table already cleared in P148's nine.
THUMB_STORE_TRIAGE.ENCODING_CEILING: ARMv4T immediate-offset stores: STR imm5<<2 max 0x7C, STRB imm5 max 0x1F, STRH imm5<<1 max 0x3E. Verified empirically: 46390 pattern matches ROM-wide, observed maxima exactly 0x7C/0x1F/0x3E, never exceeded.
THUMB_STORE_TRIAGE.B11_STRENGTHENED: owner+0xE8 (232) is NOT expressible as a Thumb immediate store -- 232>>2 = 58 > 31. No direct Thumb store can write it anywhere in the ROM. The Thumb question STRENGTHENS the B11 no-writer result. deck+0x18EC likewise unexpressible.
THUMB_STORE_TRIAGE.record_0x68: SURVIVES. 101 raw candidates ROM-wide, 2 inside known Thumb fns (both ov12, not battle). ov6's 2 raw candidates both decoded individually and both FALSE POSITIVES: 0x02152318 is the low halfword of ARM 'ldrh r6,[r2,#0x6c]'; 0x0217202C is a pointer table. Raw scan is exhaustive over bytes, so ov6 is clean regardless of DB completeness. Bonus: 0x02152310 'ldr r1,[r8,#0x68]' READS +0x68 and never writes it.
THUMB_STORE_TRIAGE.deck_0x30: NARROWED to ONE game-code candidate: 0x0206BB44 in Thumb fn 0x0206BAC8. 375 raw, 12 in known Thumb fns; 6 of the 7 arm9 hits sit BELOW the library/game boundary 0x0206ADB8 so are library code. Base register UNTRACED -- candidate only. DB-completeness caveat still applies here since 375 were not each decoded.
THUMB_STORE_TRIAGE.residual_for_all: register-offset stores (str rD,[rN,rM]) and split add+str bases are outside every sweep, for Thumb exactly as the ARM tool declares for ARM.
THUMB_STORE_TRIAGE.INDEPENDENTLY_CONFIRMED: Codex, given raw hex and no hint of the expected answer, independently agreed on all of it: STR imm5x4 max 0x7C, STRB imm5 max 0x1F, STRH imm5x2 max 0x3E; 0xE8 NOT expressible, 0x68 expressible (imm5=26); E1D266BC = LDRH r6,[r2,#0x6C]; window B = data/pointer sequence. So the ceiling closing B11 is triple-sourced: encoding tables, 46390 empirical pattern matches, and an independent decode.
THUMB_STORE_TRIAGE.UNPLANNED_CROSS_CHECK: Codex decoded EB00034E RELATIVELY as a branch to A+0xD40 without knowing the address. The instruction is at 0x0215231C, and 0x0215231C+0xD40 = 0x0215305C -- exactly the absolute target query.py reports. Two tools, one relative and one absolute, agreeing on the same byte validates the window's PLACEMENT, not just its decode.

P153_NETWORK_SESSION_GLOBAL.ANSWER: [0x0214CCF4 + 4] is the address 0x0214CCF8, referenced by EXACTLY TWO overlays: ov10 (202 refs) and ov7 (43 refs) = 245 total. ZERO refs in arm9 and zero in every other overlay. Measured by exhaustive word-aligned scan of arm9 + all 15 overlays. CONFIRMED_STATIC.

That is PLAUSIBLE -- it rests on overlay identity, not on a naming string or alloc tag for the object.
P153_NETWORK_SESSION_GLOBAL.design_note: the flag/pointer pair lives in a fixed RAM slot just below the overlay load base 0x0214CD20, so arm9 can test 'is networking up?' without linking against either overlay. Only the overlays touch the object; arm9 only reads the pointer. That is why a 24-byte function has 47 callers.
P153_NETWORK_SESSION_GLOBAL.accessor_cluster: eight leaf accessors in 0x0208C51C-0x0208C5E0 for a struct with byte flags at +0/+1 and the pointer at +4: 0x0208C51C read-pointer-nonzero (47 callers); 0x0208C538 init memset(g,0,2) then g[1]=1; 0x0208C564 TEST-AND-CLEAR g[0]; 0x0208C588 get g[0]; 0x0208C598 set g[0]=1; 0x0208C5AC get g[1]; 0x0208C5BC g[1]=1; 0x0208C5D0 g[1]=0. g[0] has test-and-clear and no plain clear = one-shot pending-event flag. g[1] is a persistent enable, initialised to 1.
P153_NETWORK_SESSION_GLOBAL.no_accessor_writes_+4: the init memset covers only 2 bytes and 0x0208C51C only reads. The writer is in ov7 or ov10 among the 245 refs; NOT TRACED.
P153_NETWORK_SESSION_GLOBAL.descriptor_paths_resolved: Path C (no session) = static word tables 0x020A1EFC / 0x020A1EBC indexed by slot. Path B (session) = ov10 0x0219B9CC / 0x0219BA00, falling back to thumb 0x0208C10C / 0x0208C114. Path A targets 0x02173004/0x02173014 remain UNATTRIBUTABLE (ov10/ov11 share 0x02172A60). So the loop takes descriptor data from the network when a session exists and from static tables otherwise. Mapping the three paths onto NAMED modes (local wireless vs online vs offline) is NOT CLAIMED -- ov7 appears in none of the six descriptor functions.
P153_NETWORK_SESSION_GLOBAL.neighbour_globals: literal words pointing into 0x0214CC00-0x0214CD20: 0x0214CCE0 (38 refs), 0x0214CCF0 (2), 0x0214CCF4 (9), 0x0214CCF8 (245), 0x0214CCFC (6), 0x0214CD00 (5). 0x0214CCFC and 0x0214CD00 are also ov7/ov10 -- the whole band looks like the networking subsystem's fixed globals.

Also a SIXTH functions.json binning gap: only 4 records in 0x0208C500-0x0208C640 but 8 leaf accessors; the 0x0208C5AC record claims 52 bytes and spans three functions (0x0208C5AC, 0x0208C5BC, 0x0208C5D0).

P154_SESSION_OBJECT.lifecycle_CONFIRMED: ov7 init at 0x021661BA-0x021661C4: [0x0214CCF8] = 0x021AA0D8 then memset(0x021AA0D8, 0, 0x1CB4). ov7 teardown at 0x0216636E-0x02166374: [0x0214CCF8] = 0, then bl 0x021671E4. So the session object is 0x021AA0D8, 0x1CB4 = 7348 bytes, zeroed on creation, address published to [0x0214CCF8+0x00], slot nulled on teardown. arm9's 0x0208C51C tests that slot.
P154_SESSION_OBJECT.PREDICTION_CONFIRMED: P153 predicted a liveness pointer with set/clear in the networking overlay BEFORE this code was read. Matched set/clear pair found exactly as predicted.
P154_SESSION_OBJECT.CENSUS_HYPOTHESIS_DEAD: 0x021AA0D8 is NOT a heap allocation -- it lies between ov10's end (0x021A7340) and ov12's base (0x021AC1C0), i.e. static RAM above the overlay images. The census attributes allocator CALL SITES via __FILE__/__FUNCTION__, so an object never allocated has no site and no tag. The queued 'census may tag it' idea was UNFALSIFIABLE BY CONSTRUCTION. Check heap-vs-static BEFORE reaching for the census.

Now supported by address, size, memset-on-init, null-on-teardown, all in the local-wireless overlay -- but no string or tag names it, and static allocation means none ever will. P154_SESSION_OBJECT.P153_REFINEMENTS: (1) the '245' figure counted pool WORDS, not accesses; actual load instructions are 117 in ov7 + 381 in ov10 = 498. Both numbers measure different things; the earlier wording conflated them. (2) 0x0214CCF8 is a STRUCT BASE, not a bare pointer slot; field +0x00 is the session pointer.
P154_SESSION_OBJECT.asymmetry: field +0x00: ov7 148 accesses / 2 stores; ov10 436 accesses / 0 stores. The online overlay only READS the session pointer; both writers are in local-wireless ov7.
P154_SESSION_OBJECT.HISTOGRAM_LIMITATION: the offset scan walks up to 8 instructions forward from each base load and does NOT track register liveness, so a reassigned base misattributes later accesses. Concretely: 0x0214CCF8 is only 0x28 bytes below ov6's base 0x0214CD20, so any offset >= 0x28 lands inside ov6's region. The histogram reports offsets up to +0xC40 in ov10. Cannot distinguish 'networking reuses ov6 RAM as scratch' from 'register reuse in the scan window'. NOTHING claimed beyond the first few words. +0x00 is robust (148/436 hits, two writers read instruction-by-instruction, plus arm9's independent accessor cluster).

P155_LIVENESS_SCAN.tool: scripts/decomp/base_offset_scan.py -- finds pc-relative loads of a target ADDRESS (ARM ldr Rd,[pc,#imm] and Thumb ldr Rd,[pc,#imm8]), walks forward up to 24 instructions recording accesses through the loaded register, and STOPS the walk the moment the base could have changed. Conservative: stops on any write to the base, any branch/call/return, any ldm/pop, on calls when the base is in r0-r3 or r12 (AAPCS), and on any encoding it cannot prove safe. Under-reports rather than misattributes.
P155_LIVENESS_SCAN.RESULT: 0x0214CCF8 is accessed ONLY at +0x00 -- ov10 394 accesses/0 stores, ov7 153 accesses/2 stores (0x021661C0 init, 0x02166372 teardown). 547 reads, 2 writes. Every other offset in P154's histogram (+0x04 through +0xC40) was REGISTER REUSE.
P155_LIVENESS_SCAN.MY_P154_CLAIM_RETRACTED: P154 said '0x0214CCF8 is a struct base, not a bare pointer slot'. WRONG, retracted. P153's original 'global pointer slot' was correct and my refinement made the record worse. I hedged the LARGE offsets in P154 and let the SMALL ones through unchallenged -- there were no other offsets at all.
P155_LIVENESS_SCAN.ARM7_BUG_caught_by_positive_control: the tool's first version reported ZERO hits for 0x0214CCF4, a base whose accessors I hand-read in P153. Cause: the arm9 image was chosen with sorted(glob(...))[0], and sorting puts arm7.bin ahead of arm9.bin -- it was scanning the ARM7 binary. My earlier ad-hoc scans used an UNSORTED glob and got arm9.bin only by luck of directory order. Fixed by naming arm9.bin explicitly and raising if absent.
P155_LIVENESS_SCAN.selftest: asserts (a) both hand-read ov7 writers of +0x00 are found, (b) no offset >= 0xC40 survives, (c) POSITIVE CONTROL: recovers +0x00/+0x01/+0x04 for 0x0214CCF4 from 9 arm9 sites. P158_DISPATCHER.node_fields: +0x0 per-frame tick handler (table[id].fn if the apply call returned nonzero, else stub 0x02159258); +0x4 -> &paramArray[id]; +0xC id halfword; +0xE duration (UNSIGNED, ldrh); +0x10 zeroed; +0x12 halfword from [[battleObj+0x1A8]+0x10]+0x182; +0x14/+0x15 both set to 1.

P158_PARAM_0x4_ANSWERED.writer: 0x02158F18 str r5,[r6,#4] -- the ONLY writer, and it writes a POINTER (r5 = paramArrayBase + id*8), not an amount.
P158_PARAM_0x4_ANSWERED.CONSEQUENCE_REFUTED: [param+0x4] is a CONSTANT read out of a static 8-byte-stride data array keyed by effect id. Nothing computes it at apply time. So P157's reframe -- 'chain scaling must be applied when [param+0x4] is written' -- is REFUTED. Chain-length damage scaling cannot live there.
P158_PARAM_0x4_ANSWERED.where_next: the 3 callers of 0x02158ED0 carry the id, so effect SELECTION happens there. If a dream attack picks a different id by chain length, it shows up in those callers.

P158_FIRST_FORMULA.terms: base = paramArray[id]+0x2 (unsigned halfword); charIdx = [battleObj+0x1E0] (SIGNED byte); stat = [[0x02172960] + charIdx*4 + 0x4C] (word); result stored unsigned halfword at node+0xE. 0x0200D12C is the known signed divide, called with r1=0xA.
P158_FIRST_FORMULA.WHY_IT_MATTERS: Every damage-side effect this campaign has measured is FLAT. This is the first place a per-character stat multiplies anything. It scales STATUS DURATION, not damage -- a higher +0x4C stat keeps burn/poison/paralysis running longer, by a fifth of the base per point.
P158_FIRST_FORMULA.edge_cases: duration is UNSIGNED (ldrh) and strh keeps only the low 16 bits, so a large base*stat product WRAPS rather than saturating. Also the ldrh r3,[r6,#0xe] at 0x02158F70 is a FRESH read after the bl, so the formula assumes 0x0200D12C does not touch that memory.

(2) duration is unsigned and strh truncates, so the product wraps rather than saturating. (3) my prompt wrongly claimed the fragment had two bl words; it had one, and Codex said so instead of inventing a second -- a wrong framing did not propagate.

P159_SELECTION_ROUTES.ROUTE_A: 3 sites (0x02157C6C, 0x02158204, 0x02158280), identical idiom: ldr r1,[pc]; lsl r0,r4,#0x10; ldrb r1,[r1,r0,lsr#16]; bl. ALL THREE resolve to the SAME 26-byte table at ov6 0x0217215C (pool words 0x02157F9C and 0x02158460 both hold it). The shift pair masks r4 to 16 bits, it does not scale.
P159_SELECTION_ROUTES.THIRD_CONFIRMATION_of_id_space: P157 counted 42 table entries from the data layout; P158 found indexing is table + id*8 with only id!=0 checked; P159's operand map tops out at exactly 41. Three independent facts: the id space is 1-41 with 0 = none.
P159_SELECTION_ROUTES.ROUTE_B: 2 sites in 0x02158B20. X = [[battleObj+0x1A8]+0x10]. X+0x173 (ldrsb) is NEGATED then sign-extended to 8 bits then zero-extended to 16; X+0x172 (ldrsb) is used as-is. Both are STAGED EFFECT IDS. +0x173 is stored negated, so a live value there is held negative; 0 still means none because the dispatcher returns on id 0.
P159_SELECTION_ROUTES.0x02158B20_IS_AN_ON_HIT_FLUSH: it applies pending HP damage (+0xE8, P157), a pending second-gauge amount (+0x130, P157), and two pending effect ids (+0x172, +0x173). One coherent function.
P159_SELECTION_ROUTES.edge_case: the exact form is (uint16_t)(int8_t)(-x), so a stored -128 yields 0xFF80, far outside 1-41. Either the field is never -128 or a guard exists elsewhere; not claimed which.

P160_OBJECT_0x02172960.what: CONFIRMED_STATIC: a pointer global with exactly TWO writes, both ov6 Thumb. Init 0x0214CD6E stores a 368-byte (0x170) object from the tagged allocator 0x0201A21C(size, __FILE__, __FUNCTION__, 0x7F), then memset 0 via 0x020517FC. Teardown 0x0214E196 nulls it after free via 0x0201B244. Lifetime = ov6 residency.
P160_OBJECT_0x02172960.only_offset_0: base_offset_scan.py over arm9+ov6+ov11: 276 accesses, 2 stores, ALL at +0x00. Liveness tracking on. Positive control (0x0214CCF4) passed, per the P155 lesson. So it is a pure pointer global, not a struct base.
P160_OBJECT_0x02172960.fields_of_the_pointee: +0x4C = base of a word array, stride 4, indexed by a character index; +0x158 = a count, used as count-1 to clamp an index; +0x15C = an index into the +0x4C array. All fit inside 0x170.
P160_OBJECT_0x02172960.cross_overlay_handle: ov6 loads at 0x0214CD20, ram_size 0x25C40, bss_size 0x100 -- so its image ends at exactly 0x02172960 and BSS runs 0x02172960-0x02172A60, ending exactly where ov10/ov11 load. 0x02172960 is the FIRST WORD of ov6's BSS. ov11 reads it 12 times; ov11 is in a different window so the two can be co-resident. Deliberate cross-overlay handle, not stale reuse.
P160_OBJECT_0x02172960.naming_ceiling: same shape as the P153 network slot -- allocate, store, null. Static analysis will not name it; the allocator's __FILE__/__FUNCTION__ pool words (0x0214D040, 0x0214D044) are the one remaining lead on its identity.

process_rules: NAME THE CONTAINING FUNCTION BEFORE BELIEVING AN OFFSET HIT. Searching by immediate offset finds every struct in the ROM with a field at that offset.

Use: git log --all --diff-filter=A -- "**/pattern*" then git show <branch>:<path>. Three loops plus the owner all work on separate branches -- a worktree-local grep checks one quarter of the record.
When two facts conflict, hold both open. Do NOT resolve it by demoting whichever one you derived yourself -- the shape of a mismatch is not evidence about which side is weaker.

WHEN AN INPUT IS RETRACTED, RE-DERIVE EVERYTHING DOWNSTREAM EXPLICITLY. Retracting a datum does not retract conclusions computed from it. Link derivations to their data (br dep add) so the taint propagates.

DO NOT DERIVE MY PRIORITIES FROM A PARTNER S EXPLANATION. I moved the same scheduling decision twice on runtimes successive accounts of a yield, both later withdrawn. Differentiated result: the active-character swap hunt stays at ordinary priority (independently motivated by the reimplementation goal AND by the unexplained bitset shift); the item-pickup counter goes back down (its only value was as a stimulus check, which DID rest on the yield story).

CARD DESIGN: when asking for a MULTI-CONDITION run, specify ONE LOG FILE PER CONDITION. GDB holds its log and discards interleaved appends from the driving script, so in-band markers vanish and segmentation falls on the receiver.

The CONFIRMED-BY-COMPOSITION label earned itself: holding "opcode == ability ID" as a deduction rather than a measurement is what made its later survival meaningful. A claim never separable from its premises cannot be said to have been tested.

TWO INDEX SPACES, ONE COLUMN NAME: chr_b-Complete-Mapping.md is ARM9/file order (12 = Luffy); Character-Mapping.md is DECK-BUILDER order (12 = Seiya). The record carries an explicit CAUTION and a naive grep returns the wrong one first. Always name which table before quoting a chr_b index.

A CAVEAT RECORDED IN PROSE DOES NOT CONSTRAIN CODE WRITTEN LATER (runtime, on their own oracle): they documented "there is no immediate read through this bridge" in a docstring, then built a positive control that required an immediate read-back.

WHEN A DOC HAS BEEN REVISED, A GREP RETURNS WHICHEVER VERSION MATCHES FIRST. Read the structure (headings, update markers), not just the matching lines. Third variant this session of "the information was already written down".

DO NOT INHERIT AN ARTIFACT WITHOUT CHECKING ITS LIFETIME. Savestates are session-local and do not survive an emulator reboot, so a doc s Reproducing section names states that may be gone. Same family as not inheriting a number without its frame.
CONFIRMING AN ABSENCE FROM ONE PLAUSIBLE LOCATION IS NOT VERIFICATION. To verify that something is not recorded, read the whole document, not the section where it would most naturally belong (P181).

CHECK THAT AN ARTIFACT EXISTS (not: assume artifacts expire). Savestates DO survive an emulator relaunch, so a relaunch is cheap recovery. A dead GDB stub, however, pauses the emulator with no way back except relaunch.

A prompt you write for your own next wake is not a safe place for addressing detail; the ledger is. Next-wake-you reads the bead; the prompt is what it would otherwise trust unchecked. Same shape as rule 6: stale instructions that look authoritative because you wrote them. (Runtime's rule, P184, after their own prompt said r5/r0 where the answer is r4.)

RULE 15: a correction is a claim. Check a narrowing against the artifact, the same way you would check the thing you are narrowing -- and when you retract, name which tool established the original and re-run it. A volunteered retraction reads as conscientious, so it gets LESS scrutiny than the claim it replaces. This is rule 3 inverted: the conflicting summary was my own, and authorship made it feel like knowledge instead of a claim.

RULE 15 addendum (runtime's diagnosis, better than mine): the cause was a DOCUMENTATION MISMATCH, not a memory lapse. My P181 commit message said 'no writer IN OV6' while the code it commits scans arm9 first, so the artifact and its own label disagreed at authorship and I consulted the label. Fix: write the scope the code HAS into the commit message and the doc title. Also: momentum toward a strong claim will bury weaker limits recorded in your own doc -- re-read the LIMITS section, not just the conclusion.

RULE 16: A PRIOR IS NOT A CHECK, and evidence that a region is UNRELIABLE is not evidence that it is IRRELEVANT. ov12 burned me at P171 with a text-widget field and I then cited that burn as the reason to skip ov12 -- which retired 21 real stores for ten iterations. If a region has fooled you once, look harder there. Also: hedging words like 'mainly' in your own summary hide items ('mainly ov12 and ov10' concealed 6 hits in four other overlays, 2 of them stores) -- count, do not characterise.

RULE 17: when you write a BINARY failure signature, check that the underlying property is binary. My residency card assumed overlays are loaded or not; ov12 is partially resident (head zeroed, +0x20000 present), so the card would have given a confident wrong answer in EITHER direction -- a head read clears it falsely, a +0x20000 read condemns all 9 falsely. Wrong shape, not underspecified.

Runtime's companion catch, worth keeping: 128/128 is exactly what a ZERO-FILLED region gives you, so a full match and nothing-there share a signature until you inspect byte content. Note the direction -- a NEGATIVE control on a POSITIVE result, the reverse of our usual use.

COUNT-DON'T-CHARACTERISE applies to a partner's SAMPLING GRID as much as to your own prose. Four of the five live stores sat at +0x19E72..+0x1A9A0; runtime had sampled +0x10000 and +0x20000 and inferred the resident region was 'around +0x20000'. My hedge word 'mainly' and their three-point sampling concealed the IDENTICAL four addresses. Two independent characterisations hiding the same set is a stronger lesson than either alone.

A positive control establishes REACH AND FIRING; it does not establish PRECISION. My +0x80 control hit was itself a false positive (register clobbered between the mov and the store) -- the scan still proved it reaches real code and fires, which is what the null needed. Two different questions; record both and let neither stand in for the other.

RULE 19 (runtime's, adopted): a control sited DOWNSTREAM of the event cannot distinguish 'never happened' from 'happened and was undone'. 0x0215AC08 is downstream of the +0x134 write, so a +0x50 null there means 'not attached AT 0x0215AC08', not 'never attached'. Same shape as a breakpoint sited before an effect, mirrored.

RULE 20 (runtime's framing): NAME THE STRUCT BEFORE AN OFFSET MEANS ANYTHING. Three offset collisions in this investigation: +0x172 in ov12, +0xE8 in ov12, and +0x134 as a function-pointer slot in the handler-table struct. We now have two distinct structs where +0x134 holds a code pointer and one where it carries a damage amount.

RULE 21: every scanner I built looks for a constant NEAR A STORE. A value passed as an ARGUMENT puts the constant next to a CALL, and no amount of store-adjacency searching will ever see it. I searched one mnemonic (orr) and reported the result as though it covered the question 'who sets bit 11'. Before reporting a search as covering a question, enumerate the CODE SHAPES that would answer it, not just the instructions you thought to grep.

RULE 22 (from runtime): a FALSE POSITIVE is a precision failure and cannot cause a miss; only RECALL failures undermine a null. So a control that fires on real code makes a null bankable even if that specific hit is wrong. Reach-and-fires is the ONLY thing a control must establish for a null. Do not weaken your own null over a precision defect.

When a scan returns uniform zeros across varied parameters, check what the scan cannot EXPRESS, not just whether it ran. My MASK class structurally could not match the one known instance -- adding a DIRECT class turned a worthless null into a controlled one.

RULE 23: when a constant has a plausible second ROLE, check the argument POSITION before assuming the role you are hunting. All 35 mov #0x134 sites were in r0, the size position for the tagged allocator 0x0201A21C -- not an offset argument at all. 0x134 = 308 = a believable struct size AND a believable field offset, which is exactly why position had to decide it.

Runtime's counterpart to my over-hedging note: they banked 'much closer to exhausted' and it took my finding to unwind it. Over-hedging sends you back over closed ground; over-claiming would have sent DJ and Fable into a patch decision on a holed premise. Same asymmetry, opposite direction -- and the second is worse because it leaves the session.

RULE 25: when every encoding search fails, question whether the VALUE IS ASSIGNED AT ALL. An accumulator built by summing an array is not a writer computing a result, so 'find the instruction that turns 512 into 384' may have no answer. Searching harder for a writer cannot find a sum.

The whole P195-P198 chain came from one question I did not ask for 14 iterations: what CODE SHAPES could produce this write? Each scan I built assumed the previous shape and varied the encoding. Runtime asked the shape question twice (argument-passing, then interior pointer) and both times it opened a class every encoding scan was blind to.

RULE 26: a breakpoint on an INTERIOR instruction cannot distinguish 'function not called' from 'function called, branch or loop body not entered'. Site an ENTRY breakpoint first, then narrow. Same family as rule 19 but about position WITHIN a function rather than position in the frame. Runtime's 0x02081ED0 null and my P188 retraction were both correct about those addresses and both silently read as being about the function.

KNOWING A RULE DOES NOT PREVENT MISAPPLYING IT TO THE WRONG VARIABLE. Runtime wrote 'a counter cap plus a busy loop is a truncation that looks like a finding' into their instrument list, then one wake later filtered on the OBJECT instead of on a non-zero TERM, got 60 zero-reads before the damage frame arrived, and that output would have read as 'every term is zero'. The rule was right and the axis was wrong. Check which VARIABLE a known rule applies to, not just whether you remembered the rule.

RULE 29: N filters make N+1 cases. Runtime filtered on (opponent object) OR (bit 15 set) -- two filters, three cases -- leaving 'executed with another object and bit 15 clear' invisible, so the run could not answer 'did it execute at all'. An unconditional counter closed it. Enumerate the cases a filter leaves unobservable before trusting its output.
RULE 30: hex arithmetic by eye is not a check. I computed the ObjMan's end as 0x022140B8 in my head; it is 0x022120B8. The containment conclusions held only because I scripted it.

RULE 31: a card that fails because its instruction is NEVER REACHED has not been tested. Record the stated failure signature as UNTESTED and the card as live-but-unreached, rather than letting an unreached null read as a refutation on the merits.

RULE 32: a CONTAINMENT test cannot catch a wrong NAME. I verified four addresses fell inside 0x0220DDE0+0x42D8, but I had assumed the 0x42D8 from the name I was trying to establish -- and a range test passes for any object large enough. The check agreed with itself. Verify an object's identity from its ALLOCATION (size + tagged strings), never from the fact that things you expect fall inside a size you assumed.

RULE 33: 'constructed by a function called from X_Create' is not 'is an X'. 0x0207C4C0 is called from Battle_ObjManCreate, receives the ColMan in r0, and allocates a THIRD object; three managers were in play where I had named one.

RULE 34: SCRIPTING A CHECK DOES NOT MAKE IT A CHECK -- what makes it one is that it COULD HAVE FAILED. Both loops ran an automated containment test against an assumed size and both presented it as verification; a range test passes for any object large enough. What settled the identity was EXACTNESS: slot indices with zero remainder, a constructor accounting for every byte of its object, and an array that fits one candidate and not the other. Three wakes and three namings to learn it.

RULE 36: query.py search-imm and search-op-imm CAP OUTPUT AT 200 LINES by default. Always pass --all, or a 'no hits in region X' conclusion is a truncation. My +0x48 sweep showed 200 of 644 and I nearly reported the missing 444 as absence. The control that caught it was 'does this search find the two hits I ALREADY KNOW' -- a known-answer control, which is the form rule 34 says to prefer.

RULE 37: before naming the object a store writes, check the base register's LIFETIME. r4 at 0x0207F87C looked like the pipeline's object until I found three reassignments before it. This is the same discipline that made the P184 r4 card correct, applied to my own claim instead of a partner's test.

RULE 38: an audit needs its own positive control. A capped-vs---all comparison that can only return 'same' is not a check; I included search-imm 0x48 (200 vs 644) to prove the method fires before trusting eight 'OK' rows.

RULE 39: when you issue a warning that will STOP a partner's run, check the whole record first, not the one finding you remembered. My entry+1 warning contradicted my own P178 and cost runtime a held run. A warning is a claim with a higher blast radius than a finding, so it needs MORE checking, not less -- the urgency that makes it worth sending is what tempts you to send it unchecked.

RULE 40: a queue item deferred many times is a signal, not a backlog entry. The {kind,id} table went nine deferrals while being load-bearing for the exact question I then got wrong. If something keeps losing to fast-lane work, ask what depends on it before deferring again.

RULE 41: I had the term-writer instruction in hand at P205 and read past it, because I was searching for a list insert and it was 0x10 away from what I was looking at. A search framed by the shape you EXPECT will skip the answer sitting beside it. The watchpoint found it in a function I had already disassembled -- so 'I read that function' is not 'I read that function for this question'.

RULE 42: A DERIVATION THAT LANDS ON THE OBSERVED VALUE FROM THE WRONG INPUTS IS THE MOST CONVINCING KIND OF WRONG. My 2<<8 = 512 and 512x0.75 = 384 reproduced the measured number exactly from a base that was really 8, and my discarded follow-up got a CONSTANT factor delta across two moves, which felt like independent confirmation. Pre-registering the prediction before the measurement is the only thing that stopped either from becoming canon. When arithmetic fits suspiciously well, write down what would falsify it BEFORE looking.

RULE 43: CHECK-THE-RECORD MUST SPAN BRANCHES. DJ asked whether prior docs covered the damage formula; a subagent found a CONFIRMED static formula I had never read, plus five key damage documents that exist ONLY on other branches. My check-the-record habit has been grepping one worktree, i.e. a fraction of the record, for the whole campaign.

RULE 44: THE UNIT IS PART OF THE SEARCH TERM. The flat damage term hid for 14+ iterations because every scan looked for 128 -- the right magnitude in raw/64 -- while the formula works in 8.8 where 2.0 is 512. A search for the right number in the wrong unit is indistinguishable from the value not existing, and it invalidates nothing about the scans themselves. Before sweeping for a magnitude, ask which unit the CODE uses at that point.

RULE 45: A MEASUREMENT AT ONE PARAMETER VALUE CANNOT DISTINGUISH A CONSTANT FROM A PROPORTION. r5/4 equals 512 exactly when r5 = 2048, so runtime's single-base trace fits both readings. When a partner reports a constant, check whether the observed base makes a proportional term numerically identical -- and name the parameter value that would separate them.

RULE 46: A WRONG MEASUREMENT IN THE RECORD CAN KILL A CORRECT HYPOTHESIS FOR THIRTY ITERATIONS. At P182 I wrote '0.750 is a clean 3/4, look for a multiply' and dropped it because the doc's second row implied a non-constant ratio. That row was a bad measurement. When a hypothesis is clean and exactly one data point refuses it, audit the data point before abandoning the hypothesis.

RULE 47: AN HP-DELTA ORACLE IS INVALID FOR ANY MOVE WITH A SIDE EFFECT. DOWN+B forces an opponent character switch, so the HP word afterwards belongs to a different character and the delta went UP by +0.578. The doc that produced the bad row had even NOTED neither of its moves was side-effect-free, without seeing that this was fatal to its own method. Read the formula, not the health bar, whenever the move does anything besides damage.
